translations.title: Tiling the Plane
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will compare areas covered by different tiling shapes and justify whether rearrangements preserve the amount of plane covered.
A tiling covers a two-dimensional region without gaps or overlaps. Equal numbers of differently shaped tiles do not necessarily cover equal areas. For a first-party model, use one small triangle as 1 area unit: a matching rhombus can be decomposed into 2 such triangles, and a matching trapezoid into 3. Consequently, three trapezoids cover 9 area units, four rhombi cover 8, and seven triangles cover 7. Compare how much area each shape type covers by decomposing the figures, not counting their colors. Then rearrange unchanged pieces to justify why a new pattern can have the same total area. Several tilings may support valid different classification or composition explanations.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Tiling a region uses shapes that cover the plane without gaps or overlap; a visible blank region may make a proposed pattern incomplete.
- Equal tile counts do not imply equal areas when the tiles differ in shape or area.
- Use a common small shape as an area unit; in the modeled tile family, triangle = 1 unit, rhombus = 2 triangles and trapezoid = 3 triangles.
- Moving, turning and recomposing unchanged tiles preserves their individual and combined areas. Explain claims by matching or decomposing actual regions.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — Compare tile colors by area, not count: In an original model, 3 red trapezoids, 4 blue rhombi and 7 green small triangles appear. Take each small triangle as 1 triangular area unit; each rhombus comprises 2 and each trapezoid 3. Red covers 3 × 3 = 9 units, blue 4 × 2 = 8, and green 7 × 1 = 7. Thus red covers the most, although it uses fewer pieces.
Example 2 — Make equal-area different-shape tilings: Two trapezoids cover 2 × 3 = 6 triangular area units; three rhombi cover 3 × 2 = 6; and six small triangles cover 6 × 1 = 6. Arrange each set to cover a region completely without gaps or overlaps. Explain why all three cover equal amounts of plane despite their different tile counts.
Student discussion — Give at least two defensible reasons for classifying four differently colored or gapped patterns, and justify whether a pattern tiles its entire target region. Design an equal-area two-shape mosaic and explain the area relationship. Drawing and argument require a teacher rubric.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Identify the tiled region, which colors represent each shape, and any uncovered gaps or overlaps.
Step 2: Choose a common area unit and show how each larger tile can be decomposed into those units.
Step 3: Multiply each shape's number of tiles by the corresponding area per tile.
Step 4: Compare the total area contributed by each shape type, not simply the counts of colored tiles.
Step 5: Explain how rotating or rearranging unchanged tiles preserves area, and justify more than one possible visual interpretation when appropriate.
translations.commonMistakes: Comparing only the number of differently sized colored tiles is not an area comparison: three trapezoids may cover more than seven smaller triangles. A pattern with uncovered gaps is not a tiling of the entire region, and a longer boundary does not prove more covered area.
translations.quickSummary: Different polygons in a tiling can cover unequal areas despite their counts. Decompose each into common units, compare covered area and justify when rearrangement preserves it.

translations.title: Finding Area by Decomposing and Rearranging
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will define area precisely, compare same-area figures and compose or decompose triangles and squares without changing the covered region.
Area is measured by equal-sized unit squares that cover a two-dimensional region without gaps or overlaps. Different-sized square tiles cannot be counted as identical area units until converted. A square of area 1 can be cut into two matching right triangles, each of area 1/2 square unit; their pieces can be rearranged into a different shape of the same area. Combining two copies of that square makes area 2, even if the pieces are moved and turned. Explain why congruent pieces have the same areas and why the sum of non-overlapping parts gives the complete area's measure.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- A precise area definition identifies the covered two-dimensional region, equal square units, and absence of gaps or overlaps.
- Figures that coincide exactly when overlaid have equal areas; composing and decomposing non-overlapping figures preserves total area.
- Two matching half-square right triangles combine into one square unit; a pair can also be rearranged into a non-square region of area 1.
- If tile sizes differ, convert their areas into the same unit before counting them together.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — Examine a tile measurement: A rectangle is covered by two 1-by-1 unit squares and four 1/2-by-1/2 squares without gaps or overlaps. Counting six tiles gives a wrong area because tile sizes differ; the correct area is 2 × 1 + 4 × (1/4) = 3 square units. Blank gaps or overlapping tiles also invalidate a direct count.
Example 2 — Triangle composition: Cut one area-1 square along a diagonal into two congruent right triangles. Each has area 1/2 square unit. Move one triangle to a different edge of the other, maintaining edge-to-edge contact and no overlap, to make a non-square figure of area 1. Four such triangles make total area 2 square units regardless of the outline.
Student construction — With one unit square and matching triangle pieces, draw two different non-square figures of area 2. Include the area of every piece and explain why movement conserves the total. Multiple valid designs require teacher review.

Description: Tangram area decomposition schematic. A square of area 1 square unit may be divided by one diagonal into two congruent right triangles. Each of those two pieces has area one-half square unit, so four copies have combined area 2 square units in any non-overlapping arrangement. The illustrated tangram-style partition is a schematic and is not a measurement scale for the half-square proof; use the stated equal triangular pieces and exact measurements for the numerical examples.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Identify the complete region and check its square-unit covering for gaps or overlaps.
Step 2: Convert any differently sized tiles into one consistent square-area unit.
Step 3: Identify matching triangle pieces and establish their areas by composing them into a known square.
Step 4: Assemble non-overlapping pieces into the requested area and add their areas.
Step 5: Compare two constructions by piece matching, show a valid rearrangement and explain conservation of area.
translations.commonMistakes: Counting a 1-by-1 square and a 1/2-by-1/2 square as the same unit gives an incorrect area. Two triangle pieces can form one whole unit square only when their combined area and fit support it. A drawing without proof that pieces do not overlap or leave gaps is insufficient for a conservation claim.
translations.quickSummary: Area counts equal square units without gaps or overlaps. Match pieces, convert mixed-size tiles to common units and rearrange triangles into different regions of the same total area.

translations.title: Reasoning to Find Area
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will reason about shaded polygon areas using matching parts, grid decomposition and rearrangement, including off-grid figures.
A shaded region can be compared with another region without counting every small square. If a small shaded square is moved from one location to another, the removed and added areas cancel and the total shaded area stays unchanged. On a grid, split a region into measurable rectangles or triangles; off a grid, calculate from labeled lengths and justify the partition. Subtract an unshaded hole only when its area is known or can be derived. A missing tilted square with unknown side lengths may instead require rearranging surrounding triangles.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Moving one shaded piece to fill an equal-sized hole preserves shaded area even when the boundary changes.
- On-grid composite area can be computed by decomposition into rectangles and triangles without individual-square counting.
- Off-grid area reasoning needs labeled base/height or matching pieces and square units.
- An enclosing-minus-missing strategy works only when missing area is known; otherwise find a valid decomposition or rearrangement.
- Every selected decomposition must use non-overlapping shaded pieces so no area is counted twice.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — Compare shifted shaded regions: A square region has area 16 square units. Region B is formed by removing a 1-by-1 shaded square from its interior and attaching that unchanged square to an outside edge. Shaded area is 16 − 1 + 1 = 16 square units, matching the original even though B has a hole and a new outer protrusion.
Example 2 — Choose a valid geometric strategy: A 6-by-6 shaded square includes an unshaded 3-by-3 square hole; shaded area is 36 − 9 = 27 square units. But if an interior tilted hole has unknown side lengths, do not subtract an invented area. Instead decompose the surrounding shaded region into four measurable triangles and add them.
Student explanation — Draw a new composite shaded figure and calculate its area in two distinct ways, or show how off-grid matching right triangles can be rearranged into a rectangle. Teacher evaluates diagrams and validity of the area-conservation argument.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Identify exactly which parts are shaded and distinguish them from enclosed unshaded holes.
Step 2: Look for matching pieces that can be shifted, or measurable non-overlapping rectangles/triangles.
Step 3: Select addition of pieces, rearrangement or enclosing-minus-missing only when all needed dimensions are justified.
Step 4: Calculate shaded area in square units and compare an independent method.
Step 5: Explain why no shaded region was double-counted or omitted, including any moved pieces or holes.
translations.commonMistakes: Counting an unshaded hole as if it were shaded makes the area too large. Assuming a tilted interior square has an easily computable area without its size is unsupported; divide the surrounding triangles and calculate their measurable areas instead.
translations.quickSummary: Compare shaded regions by matching moved pieces and reason about on-grid or off-grid areas through non-overlapping decomposition, rearrangement or justified subtraction.

translations.title: Parallelograms
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will find the area of a parallelogram by relating it to a rectangle through decomposition and rearrangement.
A parallelogram has two pairs of opposite parallel sides. Cut a right triangle from one end and move it to the other end without changing its area: the parallelogram becomes a rectangle with the same base and perpendicular height. Alternatively, enclose it in a rectangle and subtract the outside triangles. Both methods preserve area; a slanted side is not automatically the perpendicular height.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel opposite sides.
- Cut-and-move rearrangements and enclosing/subtracting arguments can turn parallelogram area into rectangle area.
- Area depends on a chosen base and its perpendicular height, not a slanted side.
- State the area in square units and explain conservation of area.
- Verify a proposed parallelogram using both pairs of parallel sides. Its opposite sides are equal and opposite angles have equal measures; a quadrilateral with only one parallel pair is a non-example.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — Cut and rearrange: A parallelogram has a horizontal base of 7 units and a perpendicular height of 4 units. Moving a right triangular end to the opposite end creates a 7-by-4 rectangle. The area is 7 × 4 = 28 square units.
Example 2 — Enclose and subtract: A parallelogram lies inside an 8-by-4 rectangle, leaving two non-overlapping right triangles outside it. Each has base 1 and height 4. The parallelogram area is 8 × 4 − 2 × (1 × 4 ÷ 2) = 32 − 4 = 28 square units.
Student check: Explain why changing the slant without changing base or perpendicular height does not change area.
Source-task investigation — Compare a four-sided figure with two parallel opposite-side pairs against a similar-looking non-example with only one pair. Defend the classification using sides and angles. Then move a vertex in an imagined dynamic parallelogram and explain, using a cut-and-rearrange diagram, why its area changes only when its base or perpendicular height changes. An original diagram explanation needs teacher assessment.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Identify a pair of opposite parallel sides and choose one as the base.
Step 2: Mark the perpendicular distance between the lines containing those sides.
Step 3: Rearrange an end triangle to form a rectangle, or enclose the shape and subtract outside triangles.
Step 4: Calculate the known rectangular area in square units.
Step 5: Justify why the cut-and-move or subtraction method covers the original region exactly once.
translations.commonMistakes: Mistaking the length of a slanted side for perpendicular height changes the area. A decomposition must avoid gaps and overlaps; a parallelogram is not a rectangle merely because its opposing sides match.
translations.quickSummary: Rearrange or enclose a parallelogram to relate its area to a rectangle. The selected base and perpendicular height give the area, not the diagonal or slanted edge.

translations.title: Bases and Heights of Parallelograms
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will identify a base of a parallelogram and its corresponding perpendicular height.
Any side of a parallelogram may be chosen as a base, but each base has its own corresponding height: the shortest perpendicular distance to the parallel opposite side. The side that looks vertical is not always the height. Two different base-height pairs produce the same area because each represents a valid rectangle rearrangement.
When comparing two students' rectangle decompositions of the same parallelogram, both must account for exactly the same covered area even if the cut is located differently. If only the perpendicular height doubles, the area doubles; if both base and height double, the area becomes four times as large.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- A base is a chosen side; its corresponding height is perpendicular to that base and the line through the opposite side.
- Slanted side length is generally not the height.
- A parallelogram admits two distinct families of base-height pairs, and valid pairs produce the same area.
- The area relationship is A = base × corresponding height.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — Choose correctly: A parallelogram has a base 6 cm and the perpendicular distance to the opposite side is 4 cm. Its area is 6 × 4 = 24 cm². A slanted 5 cm side does not replace the 4 cm height.
Example 2 — Another base: The same 24 cm² parallelogram uses a different side of length 5 cm as base. Its corresponding height must be 24 ÷ 5 = 4.8 cm, not 4 cm. Both valid pairs produce 24 cm².
Student check: Draw a slanted parallelogram with a horizontal 8-unit base and a 3-unit perpendicular height. Label both the base and the right angle.
Student exploration — Choose a base-height pair 5 by 3 with area 15 square units. Keep base 5 fixed and double height to 6: area is 30; double both 5 and 3 to 10 and 6: area is 60. Show a perpendicular segment and explain why using a slanted 5-unit side as the height would not establish either result. Teacher reviews the labeled drawing.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Pick one entire side to serve as the base.
Step 2: Draw a perpendicular from the line of that base to the opposite parallel side.
Step 3: Confirm the height segment meets the base direction at 90°, even if outside the drawn region.
Step 4: Multiply the selected base length by its corresponding height when an area is required.
Step 5: Check a different valid base-height pair if available; it should give the same area.
translations.commonMistakes: The slanted side is not automatically the altitude. Do not mix the length of one possible base with a height corresponding to the other base; the resulting product need not equal the area.
translations.quickSummary: A base is any chosen side of a parallelogram; its height is the perpendicular distance to the opposite side. Match each base with its own height.

translations.title: Area of Parallelograms
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will use a valid base-height pair to find the area or a missing dimension of a parallelogram.
Rearranging a parallelogram into a rectangle establishes the area formula A = b × h, where h is perpendicular to the chosen base. You can find a missing base or height by division when the area and the other dimension are known. Parallelograms with the same base and perpendicular height have the same area even if they lean differently.
Two different, noncongruent parallelograms can have the same area when their base-height products are equal. When a composite picture includes four matching shaded parallelograms around an unshaded central region, find the central area by calculating the outer total and subtracting exactly the four shaded parts; do not invent dimensions from an undimensioned diagram.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- For every parallelogram, area = base × corresponding perpendicular height.
- If area and one measurement are known, divide to find the other.
- Valid pairs must correspond to the same base direction, and area units are squared.
- Different slants can have identical area.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — Area: A parallelogram has a horizontal base of 9 cm and perpendicular height of 5 cm. Its area is 9 × 5 = 45 cm².
Example 2 — Missing base: A parallelogram has area 60 m² and perpendicular height 4 m. Its matching base is 60 ÷ 4 = 15 m.
Student check: Two parallelograms lean in opposite directions but both have base 6 cm and height 3 cm. Explain why both have area 18 cm².
Student investigation — Sketch two parallelograms with different slants and one shared base of 6 cm and perpendicular height of 3 cm. Both have area 18 cm²; their outlines need not coincide. For an unshaded central region surrounded by four equal-area shaded parallelograms, write 'outer area minus four times one shaded area' with the known measurements and explain which additional lengths are needed before computing a number.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Select a base and locate the perpendicular height that goes with it.
Step 2: Write A = b × h with labeled units.
Step 3: Multiply to find A, or divide A by the given dimension to find a missing positive dimension.
Step 4: Check by substituting the result back into A = b × h.
Step 5: Explain why changing only the slant leaves the area unchanged.
translations.commonMistakes: Using the length of a diagonal or slanted side in place of the perpendicular altitude can be wrong. A base has length units; an area has square units.
translations.quickSummary: Parallelogram area is b × h for a corresponding perpendicular height. Divide the area by a known dimension to recover the missing base or height.

translations.title: From Parallelograms to Triangles
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will relate triangles and parallelograms by composing two matching triangles into one parallelogram.
A diagonal divides a parallelogram into two triangles that match exactly. Conversely, two identical copies of any triangle can be moved and rotated to form a parallelogram. Since the two triangles have equal area, each occupies half of the constructed parallelogram, providing the reasoning behind the triangle area formula.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Two identical copies of a triangle can compose a parallelogram without gaps or overlap.
- A diagonal partitions a parallelogram into two equal-area triangles.
- Triangle area is half the area of the associated parallelogram with the same base and perpendicular height.
- A rearrangement argument is required; do not infer equality only from visual appearance.
- A diagonal splits any parallelogram into two congruent triangles. Two congruent copies of any triangle form a parallelogram, but a rectangular result requires an appropriate right-triangle arrangement; not every triangle pair makes a rectangle.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — Split a parallelogram: A parallelogram has base 8 cm and height 5 cm. Its area is 8 × 5 = 40 cm². Its diagonal divides it into two matching triangles, each with area 20 cm².
Example 2 — Compose a parallelogram: Two identical triangles each have area 12 cm². When arranged without overlap as a parallelogram, the parallelogram has total area 24 cm².
Student check: Explain with two paper triangle cutouts why the area of one triangle is half the constructed parallelogram's area.
Student reasoning — Draw a scalene non-right triangle and rotate a matching copy through a half-turn to make a parallelogram, then repeat with a right triangle to make a rectangle. Explain why the first two matching triangles do not form a rectangle simply because the pieces are congruent. Original constructions require diagram/teacher review.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Create or identify two matching copies of a triangle.
Step 2: Turn one copy and join it with the other along the appropriate side to form a parallelogram.
Step 3: Confirm that the parts neither overlap nor leave uncovered gaps.
Step 4: Find the parallelogram area from its base and perpendicular height.
Step 5: Divide by two and explain why the triangles must have equal area.
translations.commonMistakes: Joining non-matching triangles does not guarantee an equal-halves parallelogram. The relevant height remains perpendicular to the base, not simply a triangle's longest side.
translations.quickSummary: Two identical triangles make a parallelogram. One triangle occupies half the area, leading to A = (base × perpendicular height) ÷ 2.

translations.title: Area of Triangles
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will use area conservation and parallelogram reasoning to find the area of a triangle.
Double a triangle to make a parallelogram with the same base and perpendicular height. The combined area is base × height, so the original triangle has half that area. This argument works for triangles that are not drawn on a grid and for obtuse triangles whose altitude can fall outside the triangle.
Another source-aligned strategy cuts a triangle into smaller shapes that can be shifted into a parallelogram. If the new parallelogram contains exactly the original triangle's pieces with no overlap or loss, the two regions have equal area; do not automatically divide that new parallelogram's area by two. The factor one-half applies only when you create a parallelogram from TWO entire matching copies of the triangle.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- A triangle's area is half of the area of a parallelogram formed from two matching copies.
- The height is perpendicular to the line through the selected base.
- Triangle area is A = (b × h) ÷ 2 in square units.
- Shapes with equal base lengths and perpendicular heights have equal areas.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — Triangle area: A triangle has base 8 cm and perpendicular height 5 cm. Doubling it makes a parallelogram of area 8 × 5 = 40 cm². The triangle area is 40 ÷ 2 = 20 cm².
Example 2 — Same area, different shape: Two different triangles each have base 10 m and corresponding perpendicular height 4 m. Both have area 10 × 4 ÷ 2 = 20 m² even if one is scalene and one is obtuse.
Student check: Draw or describe two identical triangles that form a parallelogram, and explain why dividing the area by two is justified.
Student dissection — Start with one triangle, cut it into a smaller triangle and a trapezoid, and rearrange those two pieces to make a parallelogram. Because the pieces are conserved, the new parallelogram has the SAME area as the original triangle. Contrast this with the separate method of duplicating the WHOLE triangle: that doubled parallelogram has TWICE the original triangle's area. Teacher reviews that the two transformations are not conflated.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Choose a base and identify its corresponding perpendicular height.
Step 2: Imagine or draw a matching triangle to complete a parallelogram.
Step 3: Compute the parallelogram area b × h.
Step 4: Divide that total by two for the area of one triangle.
Step 5: Check the square units and explain why two identical triangles give two equal regions.
translations.commonMistakes: Multiplying the base by a slanted edge rather than the perpendicular height mismeasures area. Forgetting to divide by two gives the area of the doubled parallelogram, not one triangle.
translations.quickSummary: A triangle is half of its matching parallelogram: A = (b × h) ÷ 2. The height must be perpendicular to the chosen base.

lessons.sourceTitle: Open Up Resources 6–8 Math / IM 6–8 Math

translations.title: Formula for the Area of a Triangle
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will justify and use the general triangle-area formula from base and perpendicular height.
The area of any triangle is half the area of a corresponding parallelogram: A = ½bh. A triangle has three choices of base, and each requires its corresponding height. The formula follows from area conservation when two matching triangles compose a parallelogram, not from memorizing a rule without a diagram or argument.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Triangle area formula: A = ½ × base × corresponding perpendicular height.
- Every side may be selected as a base, but the paired height must be perpendicular to it.
- Two matching triangles compose a parallelogram, justifying the factor ½.
- Rearranging the formula allows a missing base or height to be found.
- A height is the perpendicular distance between the line containing the chosen base and a parallel line through the opposite vertex. An illustrative perpendicular measurement segment need not itself pass through the opposite vertex if it spans those same parallel lines; the usual altitude does pass through the vertex.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — Apply the formula: A triangle has base 10 cm and perpendicular height 6 cm. Its area is ½ × 10 × 6 = 30 cm².
Example 2 — Recover a base: A triangle's area is 30 m² and its corresponding height is 5 m. Since 30 = ½ × b × 5, the base is (2 × 30) ÷ 5 = 12 m.
Student check: Explain why a triangle with base 12 and height 5 has the same area as a triangle with base 10 and height 6.
Student verification — For a triangle with a horizontal 6-cm base and an opposite vertex 4 cm above the base line, draw one 4-cm perpendicular through the vertex and another 4-cm perpendicular between the same two parallel lines at a different horizontal position. Both show the corresponding height 4 cm; the area stays ½ × 6 × 4 = 12 cm². Mark the right angles and explain the distinction between the actual altitude and an equivalent translated height segment.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Select a triangle side as a base and identify its perpendicular height.
Step 2: Explain or sketch how two identical copies form a parallelogram.
Step 3: Write 2A = b × h, then A = ½bh.
Step 4: Substitute known lengths or rearrange the formula for an unknown length.
Step 5: Verify the area in square units or the missing length in linear units.
translations.commonMistakes: The triangle area is not b × h; that is the area of the doubled parallelogram. Do not combine a base with a height measured relative to a different base.
translations.quickSummary: All triangles satisfy A = ½bh using a base and its corresponding perpendicular height. The factor ½ follows from pairing identical triangles.

lessons.sourceTitle: Open Up Resources 6–8 Math / IM 6–8 Math

translations.title: Bases and Heights of Triangles
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will draw and identify a triangle's height perpendicular to a chosen base, including when the height lies outside the triangle.
For every chosen side of a triangle, the corresponding height is the perpendicular distance from the opposite vertex to the line containing the base. It can meet a base segment or an extension of the line through that segment, particularly for an obtuse triangle. Only a matching base and height may be used in A = ½bh.
A square corner or the right angle of an index card can be aligned with the chosen base line and slid until its perpendicular edge meets the opposite vertex. Rotate the SAME triangle to try different side choices: all three valid base-height products should give the same double area, even when one height falls outside the polygon.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- A height runs perpendicular from the opposite vertex to the line through the chosen base.
- An altitude may lie outside the triangle if the perpendicular meets an extended base line.
- A slanted side is not automatically the altitude.
- Choose the most convenient valid base-height pair for area calculations.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — Perpendicular height: A triangle has horizontal base 7 cm and a vertex 4 cm above the base line. The corresponding height is 4 cm, so its area is ½ × 7 × 4 = 14 cm².
Example 2 — Not a height: A slanted side measures 5 cm, but its angle with the chosen base is not 90°. It cannot be used as that base's height. If the actual perpendicular height is 3 cm and the base 8 cm, the area is 12 cm².
Student check: For an obtuse triangle, draw an extension of one base and mark the right angle at the foot of its perpendicular altitude.
Construction check — Draw a non-right triangle of area 12 square units by choosing base 6 units and perpendicular height 4 units; explain why ½ × 6 × 4 = 12. Rotate it, label each of its three sides as a possible base in turn, and use an index card's right-angle corner to locate or extend each corresponding perpendicular height. Teacher reviews the three drawings rather than accepting an unverified height label.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Choose and mark the side used as the base.
Step 2: Extend the line containing that base if necessary.
Step 3: Drop a perpendicular from the opposite vertex to that line and mark the 90° angle.
Step 4: Measure the perpendicular segment as height; multiply by the chosen base and divide by two if finding area.
Step 5: Confirm the base and height are paired and record square units for area.
translations.commonMistakes: A height need not be entirely inside a triangle. Measuring a slanted side or drawing a vertical segment that is not perpendicular to the selected base can produce a false area.
translations.quickSummary: The height corresponding to a triangle base is its perpendicular distance from the opposite vertex to the base line, which may need extension.

lessons.sourceTitle: Open Up Resources 6–8 Math / IM 6–8 Math

translations.title: Polygons
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will identify polygons using precise geometric criteria, select area strategies for unfamiliar quadrilaterals, and justify a trapezoid area formula.
A polygon is a closed two-dimensional figure whose boundary consists of straight line segments, each meeting just one other segment at each endpoint and never crossing elsewhere. It encloses a region; when mathematicians speak of a polygon's area they mean the area of that enclosed region. A collection of intersecting or disconnected triangles does not automatically form one polygon. After classifying examples and counterexamples, choose two non-parallelogram quadrilaterals and plan a valid area calculation by triangulating, rearranging, or enclosing and subtracting. For a trapezoid with parallel bases a and b and perpendicular height h, two congruent copies can form a parallelogram with base a+b and height h; therefore one trapezoid has area (a+b)h/2. Source work also includes partner discussion of alternative plans and an optional pinwheel-shaped shaded region; diagrams and justifications need teacher review, not only an area number.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- A simple polygon is closed, made of connected straight sides, and has sides that meet only at common endpoints; a self-crossing path or several disconnected figures is not one simple polygon.
- The region enclosed by a polygon can be decomposed into triangles and rectangles with no overlapping interiors; use perpendicular heights in area formulas.
- There may be several defensible first moves for an unfamiliar quadrilateral: partition it, duplicate a triangle, rearrange pieces, or enclose and subtract.
- For a trapezoid with parallel bases a and b and perpendicular height h, its area is (a+b)h/2. This follows by combining two congruent copies into a parallelogram with base a+b.
- A complex shaded pinwheel can be decomposed into measurable non-overlapping sections or subtracted from a known enclosure; justify every measured length and preserve square units.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — Polygons and non-polygons: A closed five-segment boundary whose edges meet only at consecutive endpoints is a simple pentagon. An open zigzag is not closed; a circle has a curved edge; two triangles touching at only one vertex do not form the boundary of one simple polygon. Name each reason and compare with a classmate who used a different correct classification criterion.
Example 2 — Derive trapezoid area: A trapezoid has parallel bases 8 cm and 4 cm and perpendicular height 3 cm. Pair two identical copies to construct a parallelogram with base 8+4=12 cm and height 3 cm. Its area is 12×3=36 cm², so one trapezoid has area 18 cm². Independently decompose it into a 4-by-3 rectangle (12 cm²) plus two right triangles, each base 2 and height 3 (3 cm² each), totaling 18 cm².
Example 3 — Choose an area strategy for a composite pinwheel: Description: Draw an original square-shaped pinwheel region formed by a central 2-by-2 square and four non-overlapping right triangular wings, one outside each side, each with base 2 and perpendicular height 2. Count its central area 4 square units and each wing 2 square units; total area 4+4×2=12 square units. The construction is an original illustrative alternative, NOT the historical publisher's exact pinwheel drawing. A teacher reviews whether the diagram actually places wings without overlap and whether another decomposition gives the same area.
Partner activity — Choose two different labeled quadrilaterals and share only the first two or three planned area moves before calculating. Discuss alternative valid plans, then compute with supported dimensions. Classify several original closed, open and crossing boundaries; explain each decision and how the selected pieces could be triangulated.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Check whether each proposed polygon is a single closed, non-self-crossing chain of straight segments and justify the classification.
Step 2: For an unfamiliar quadrilateral, choose a defensible first move: decompose, duplicate a piece, rearrange, or enclose the region.
Step 3: Identify base lengths and corresponding perpendicular heights of all non-overlapping triangles, rectangles or trapezoids used in the plan.
Step 4: Add the included areas, or subtract known excluded pieces; verify the trapezoid identity (a+b)h/2 by joining two copies.
Step 5: State the area in square units and compare a different valid method; preserve all measured lengths and avoid inventing missing diagram values.
translations.commonMistakes: A self-crossing boundary, disconnected set of segments, or curved edge is not a simple polygon. The area of a trapezoid is NOT (a+b)×h unless both congruent copies are counted; divide by two for one. Do not assume a slanted side is a perpendicular height or use an unmeasured diagonal as if it were one unit long. Original pinwheel drawings and explanations require geometric evidence and teacher judgement; a bare numerical answer is insufficient.
translations.quickSummary: Classify simple polygons by straight, closed, non-self-crossing boundaries. Find unfamiliar quadrilateral and pinwheel areas by justified decomposition or enclosure; the trapezoid formula (a+b)h/2 follows from pairing congruent copies.

lessons.sourceTitle: Open Up Resources 6–8 Math / IM 6–8 Math

translations.title: What is Surface Area?
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will estimate and calculate the surface area of exposed faces, including an uncovered cabinet bottom and alternative arrangements of unit cubes.
Surface area measures the total exposed area of the faces of a three-dimensional object in square units. To cover a cabinet with equal square notes, count the notes needed on each face that actually requires covering; a cabinet resting on the floor may have an excluded bottom. Estimate before computing and identify which dimensions and unit-square size are needed. For a closed rectangular prism with edge lengths a, b and c, all six outside faces have total area 2(ab + ac + bc). Build a different prism from the same 12 unit cubes and compare its exposed face count: equal volume does not imply equal surface area. Any learner-created cube arrangement and explanation requires teacher review.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Surface area is the sum of every exposed face's area in square units; explicitly exclude any face that the problem says is not covered.
- A closed rectangular prism has three opposite pairs of equal-area faces and surface area 2(ab + ac + bc).
- For a cabinet without a covered bottom, add the top and four side faces only; compute coverage in consistent square-tile units.
- Rearranging 12 equal unit cubes into prisms with different dimensions preserves volume (12 cubic units) but can change surface area; touching interior faces are not exposed.
- Drawings, coverings, estimates and original three-dimensional constructions demand justified, often teacher-reviewed reasoning.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — Cover an open-bottom cabinet: An original rectangular cabinet model measures 8 square-note widths along the front, 5 along the side and 3 notes high. The uncovered bottom is excluded. The top needs 8 × 5 = 40 notes, the front and back need 2 × (8 × 3) = 48, and the side faces need 2 × (5 × 3) = 30. Total covered outside area is 40 + 48 + 30 = 118 square-note units. A closed cabinet would additionally need 40 for the bottom, giving 158.
Example 2 — Rearrange 12 identical cubes: A 2-by-2-by-3 prism has 12 cubic units of volume and exposed area 2(2×2 + 2×3 + 2×3) = 32 square units. A 1-by-2-by-6 prism still contains 12 cubes but has surface area 2(1×2 + 1×6 + 2×6) = 40 square units. The second prism exposes eight more unit square faces.
Student construction — Describe or model a third rectangular prism made from 12 unit cubes; give its dimensions and count every exposed face. Explain why its volume is still 12 cubic units. A teacher reviews the drawing/model and explanation rather than scoring only a target number.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Identify the intended solid and precisely which outer faces are to be covered or excluded.
Step 2: Record consistent linear measurements and the size of one square covering unit.
Step 3: Calculate each face area and multiply for any opposite matching face pairs, excluding the bottom when specified.
Step 4: Add only exposed face areas; for an alternative cube assembly, count unit cubes separately from exposed unit squares.
Step 5: Check the surface-area units, justify why each face was counted once and explain how changing cube arrangement can change coverage without changing volume.
translations.commonMistakes: Blindly applying the six-face formula to a cabinet whose bottom is not being covered overcounts its surface. Counting only three visible faces from a drawing undercounts a closed prism. Counting touching internal cube faces also inflates area; volume is the count of unit cubes, not the count of outside square faces.
translations.quickSummary: Surface area counts exposed square faces. Exclude specified uncovered faces, add all remaining face areas and compare cube constructions without confusing constant volume with potentially different surface area.

lessons.sourceTitle: Open Up Resources 6–8 Math / IM 6–8 Math

translations.title: Polyhedra
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will distinguish prisms, pyramids, and other polyhedra by their polygonal faces, edges, vertices and nets.
A polyhedron is a three-dimensional solid enclosed by flat polygonal faces. Adjacent faces meet along edges, and edges meet at vertices. A prism has two matching parallel polygonal bases joined by lateral faces, while a pyramid has one polygonal base whose triangular side faces meet at one apex. A net is a plane arrangement of faces that folds to create the solid; not every collection of correct face shapes folds without overlap.
Source activity extension: First sort a collection of three-dimensional solids and non-solids, including a cylinder or sphere whose surfaces are curved. Explain the features that distinguish polyhedra. Next select more than one valid net for a prism or pyramid using precisely the needed polygons and shared edges, and check whether folding joins all edges. Physical cutting, folding, gluing, and assembly are meaningful source tasks; the original student-created construction requires accessible directions and teacher evaluation.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Polyhedra are closed solids bounded by flat polygonal faces.
- Prisms have two congruent parallel polygonal bases; pyramids have one base and an apex.
- Nets must include every face and have connections that allow folding without overlap.
- Count faces, edges and vertices separately; a net is a two-dimensional representation of a three-dimensional solid.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — Triangular prism: A triangular prism has 2 triangular bases and 3 rectangular lateral faces, or 5 faces in total. A useful net contains exactly those five polygons with shared edges that can fold correctly.
Example 2 — Square pyramid: A square pyramid has a square base and 4 triangular sides, again 5 faces. It differs from the triangular prism even though both have five faces.
Student check: Sketch a five-polygon net for each solid and explain how the polygons would meet at edges when folded.
Example 3 — Foldable nets and the smallest polyhedron: Description: A tetrahedron has four triangular faces, six edges, and four vertices. One possible net uses one central triangle with three other triangles attached, one along each of its three edges, and can fold into a triangular pyramid. Fewer than four flat polygonal faces cannot bound a three-dimensional region. By contrast, four triangles connected only at isolated vertices do not form a foldable net. Model or describe a second valid arrangement; a teacher checks foldability and connectivity.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Determine whether the object has only flat polygonal faces.
Step 2: Identify the base or bases and count the remaining lateral faces.
Step 3: Describe how faces meet along edges and where the vertices are.
Step 4: Draw or analyze a net with the correct polygons and suitable edge connections.
Step 5: Check that the net could fold without gaps or overlapping faces, and name the solid.
translations.commonMistakes: Matching the number of faces does not prove two polyhedra are the same. A picture of separate polygons is not necessarily a valid net; face connectivity and folding matter. A cylinder is not a polyhedron because its curved surface is not a polygon; a shape made of the right face counts can still have an invalid net if their attached edges cannot fold into the assigned solid.
translations.quickSummary: Polyhedra have flat polygonal faces meeting at edges and vertices. A prism has two matching parallel bases; a pyramid has one base and an apex. Nets represent foldable surfaces.

lessons.sourceTitle: Open Up Resources 6–8 Math / IM 6–8 Math

translations.title: Nets and Surface Area
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will match polyhedra to nets and use the face areas shown by a net to calculate surface area.
A net is a two-dimensional arrangement of polygons that can be folded into a three-dimensional solid. Every exposed face of a prism or pyramid must appear exactly once. To find surface area, measure the area of each polygon in the net, then add the results in square units. A net needs correct adjacency as well as the right number and shapes of faces.
Source activity extension: Before calculating, match a supplied net to its intended three-dimensional shape and justify whether it is a rectangular prism or a triangular prism. Decide which nets actually fold without face overlap; then label every face and calculate the surface area of the folded solid. Different face arrangements can describe the same prism, so an original foldable net is assessed by the geometry and face connectivity, not just the face-area sum.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- A valid net folds along edges into the intended solid without gaps or overlapping faces.
- A solid's surface area is the sum of the areas of its exposed faces.
- For a rectangular prism, count both members of each of its three matching face pairs.
- For a pyramid, count one polygonal base and each triangular lateral face.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — Rectangular prism net: A 4-by-3-by-2 box has two 4-by-3 rectangles, two 4-by-2 rectangles and two 3-by-2 rectangles. Surface area is 2(12) + 2(8) + 2(6) = 52 square units.
Example 2 — Square pyramid net: A pyramid with a square base of side 4 and four triangular faces each with base 4 and perpendicular face height 3 has total surface area 4 × 4 + 4 × (½ × 4 × 3) = 16 + 24 = 40 square units.
Student check: Explain how each polygon of a net represents exactly one outside face of the folded solid.
Example 3 — Distinguish two prism nets: Description: A rectangular prism with dimensions 4,3,2 has six rectangular faces in pairs (4×3 twice), (4×2 twice), and (3×2 twice); its surface area is 24+16+12=52 square units. A triangular prism instead has two congruent triangular bases and three rectangular lateral faces. A layout of six rectangles cannot be a triangular prism net; a correct five-face triangular-prism net has two matching triangles and three rectangles whose shared edges can close without gaps. Teacher checks the student-drawn net, not only 52.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Identify the solid and list all outside faces by polygon type.
Step 2: Check that the net contains each face exactly once with foldable edge connections.
Step 3: Identify each face's necessary base and perpendicular height or length and width.
Step 4: Calculate every face area and sum in square units.
Step 5: Explain why this net can represent the solid and confirm that no face was omitted or counted twice.
translations.commonMistakes: A group of polygons is not necessarily a foldable net. Missing a hidden face or using the sloping edge instead of a perpendicular triangle height gives an incorrect surface area. Some proposed nets with all the correct faces still fold with overlaps or fail to close; face inventory is necessary but not sufficient. Compare actual attached edges.
translations.quickSummary: A net unfolds a polyhedron into its faces. Match the faces correctly and add all face areas in square units to find surface area.

lessons.sourceTitle: Open Up Resources 6–8 Math / IM 6–8 Math

translations.title: More Nets, More Surface Area
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will draw, label and validate nets of polyhedra, calculate surface areas, and compare the resulting boxes' capacities.
A net must contain each exterior polygon exactly once and connect adjacent faces so it folds into the named prism or pyramid without overlap. Draw a net at an indicated scale and mark each face, its dimensions and its neighboring edges. Total surface area is the sum of all exposed face areas; volume measures the number of cubic units a closed box holds. Two boxes may have the same volume but different surface areas, or the same surface area but different volumes. An original student-built net, choice of flap placement or visual explanation cannot be verified by one numerical answer and needs teacher review.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- A valid polyhedron net includes all exterior faces with correct connectivity, matching edge lengths and no overlapping folded faces.
- Surface area is the sum of all polygon face areas on the net, measured in square units; prism volume measures enclosed cubic units.
- A triangular prism requires two congruent triangular bases plus three rectangular lateral faces; a square pyramid has one square base and four triangular side faces.
- Comparing nets of boxes requires independent surface-area and volume calculations; equal surface area does not force equal capacity or vice versa.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — Triangular prism net: A right-triangular-prism has two congruent triangle bases with legs 3 cm and 4 cm, hypotenuse 5 cm, and prism length 6 cm. Each triangle has area 3×4÷2=6 cm². The three rectangular lateral faces have areas 3×6=18, 4×6=24 and 5×6=30 cm². The complete net has surface area 2×6+18+24+30=84 cm². Check that the five polygons form a connected, foldable net rather than five disjoint shapes.
Example 2 — Compare boxes: A closed 2-by-3-by-6 cm prism has volume 36 cm³ and surface area 2(6+12+18)=72 cm²; a 3-by-3-by-4 cm prism also has volume 36 cm³ but surface area 2(9+12+12)=66 cm². The second uses less cardboard for the same capacity in this ideal model. Their nets must still show all six faces and the required matching edge connections.
Student net construction — Draw a valid cube net different from a given first-party example, and a triangular prism net labeled with its dimensions. Explain how each polygon would meet its neighbors when folded and why the resulting surface area has square units. Teacher reviews foldability and geometric justification.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Identify the polyhedron, all exposed face polygons and the edge lengths from the given drawing.
Step 2: Draw one polygon for every face with correct dimensions and connected matching edges.
Step 3: Validate by reasoning how the net folds without missing faces or overlap.
Step 4: Compute each face area and add for total square-unit surface area; separately multiply the three prism dimensions if volume is requested.
Step 5: Compare boxes using both their area and capacity, checking dimension units and explaining the construction or volume-area distinction.
translations.commonMistakes: A set of correctly sized polygons with the wrong shared edges is not necessarily a valid net. Counting only three visible faces ignores hidden exterior faces. Computing volume from a net and reporting cubic units as if it were its surface area confuses different attributes. Equal capacities do not guarantee equal cardboard usage.
translations.quickSummary: Draw a complete foldable net and sum every exterior polygon's area. Compare rectangular boxes by both square-unit covering and cubic-unit capacity; a correct original net needs visual review.

lessons.sourceTitle: Open Up Resources 6–8 Math / IM 6–8 Math

translations.title: Distinguishing Between Surface Area and Volume
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will distinguish linear length, square-area covering and cubic volume, and compare solids with equal volumes or equal surface areas.
Length is measured in linear units, area and outer surface area in square units, and volume in cubic units. Rebuild two different solids from the same eight unit cubes: both must have volume 8 cubic units, but the number of external square faces can differ. Conversely, different rectangular prisms can have identical surface area but different volumes. For example, a 1-by-1-by-5 prism and a 1-by-2-by-3 prism both have surface area 22 square units but their volumes are 5 and 6 cubic units. Count all exterior faces including hidden ones, not the internal contact faces between cubes; explain the distinction with a labeled drawing or model.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- One-dimensional lengths use linear units, two-dimensional surface areas use square units, and three-dimensional volumes use cubic units.
- Solids made from the same eight unit cubes have equal volume 8 cubic units but may expose different numbers of unit-square faces.
- Equal surface area does not imply equal volume; different shapes may have the same total face area yet contain different cubic amounts.
- Internal square contacts between touching cubes are not exposed, while exterior faces hidden from one viewpoint still count.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — Eight cubes arranged differently: A 2-by-2-by-2 cube contains eight unit cubes and has surface area 6×4=24 square units. An elongated 1-by-2-by-4 prism also contains eight cubes but has surface area 2(1×2+1×4+2×4)=28 square units. A 1-by-1-by-8 prism exposes 2(1+8+8)=34 square units. These three solids all have equal volume 8 cubic units, with surface areas 24, 28 and 34.
Example 2 — Same surface area, different volumes: A 1-by-1-by-5 cm prism has area 2(1+5+5)=22 cm² and volume 5 cm³. A 1-by-2-by-3 cm prism has area 2(2+3+6)=22 cm² and volume 6 cm³. Thus equal surface area does not force equal volume; the units alone show these are different properties.
Student construction — Use eight identical cube blocks to create two distinct connected solids, record each volume and exposed surface area, and create a labeled text or diagram representation. Then give an example of two prisms of equal surface area but different volume. Teacher checks the construction and systematic exposed-face counting.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: State whether the measured attribute is length, exterior face coverage, or enclosed three-dimensional space and choose the corresponding unit.
Step 2: For an eight-unit-cube assembly, count unit cubes for volume and count only external squares for surface area.
Step 3: Record every visible and hidden external face without counting internal contacts twice.
Step 4: For two rectangular prisms, calculate 2(ab+ac+bc) and abc separately and identify which quantities are equal or different.
Step 5: Explain with correct units and original labeled models why equal volume and equal area are logically independent.
translations.commonMistakes: Equal volume never guarantees equal surface area, and equal surface area never guarantees equal volume. Counting the touching internal faces between two cubes overestimates exposed area. Reporting 22 cm³ as the outside surface of the prisms confuses cubic volume units with square area units; also do not ignore faces hidden by perspective.
translations.quickSummary: Surface area and volume describe different dimensions. Eight-cube designs share a volume but can have different exposed areas; two prisms can also share area 22 yet have different volumes 5 and 6.

lessons.sourceTitle: Open Up Resources 6–8 Math / IM 6–8 Math

translations.title: Squares and Cubes
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will connect squares and cubes with repeated multiplication and interpret exponents of 2 and 3.
A square with side length s has area s × s = s² square units. A cube with edge length s has volume s × s × s = s³ cubic units. The exponent tells how many equal factors are multiplied; it does not mean multiply the base by the exponent. When an area or volume is a perfect square or cube, find the corresponding whole-number side length by reasoning backwards.
Source activity extension: Model square and cube numbers with physical or digitally manipulable unit tiles and unit cubes. Given 32 identical unit cubes, the largest complete single cube uses 3×3×3=27 cubes and leaves 5 unused; 4×4×4=64 cannot fit. With 64 unit cubes, a 4×4×4 cube uses all 64. Count unit cubes in layers, then distinguish one face's area from volume. Identify perfect squares, perfect cubes and powers that can represent both.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- s² means s × s and measures area of a square with side s.
- s³ means s × s × s and measures volume of a cube with edge s.
- For whole-number edges, the resulting areas are perfect squares and volumes are perfect cubes.
- Report the square or cubic units that correspond to the geometry.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — Square area: A square has side length 5 cm. Its area is 5² = 5 × 5 = 25 cm²; conversely, a square of area 25 cm² has side 5 cm.
Example 2 — Cube volume: A cube has edge length 4 m. Volume is 4³ = 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 m³. A cube of volume 64 m³ has edge 4 m.
Student check: Explain why 3³ is 27 rather than 9, using three stacked 3-by-3 layers.
Example 3 — Build the largest cube: Description: Display 32 identical 1-by-1-by-1 unit cubes in a movable inventory. A cube of edge 3 needs 3 layers of 3×3=9 cubes, or 27; 5 remain. Edge 4 would require 4 layers of 4×4=16, or 64, so it cannot be constructed with 32 cubes. With 64 cubes, construct edge 4 using all 64. For the 3-cube-edge model one face covers 3²=9 square units and its volume is 3³=27 cubic units; for edge 4 each face is 16 square units and volume 64 cubic units. Teacher checks the model/accessible coordinate-layer alternative.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Determine whether the model is a square face or a three-dimensional cube.
Step 2: Identify the shared side or edge length s.
Step 3: Write the appropriate repeated product s × s or s × s × s.
Step 4: Evaluate it or work backwards to identify a whole-number edge length.
Step 5: State square units for area or cubic units for volume and interpret the exponent geometrically.
translations.commonMistakes: 3³ does not mean 3 × 3; it means three factors of 3. Square-unit area cannot replace cubic-unit volume. Using all 32 cubes does not make a cube because 32 is not a perfect cube; count complete equal square layers, not just a pile of cubes. A square number describes a face, a cube number a three-dimensional total.
translations.quickSummary: A square's area is s² and a cube's volume is s³. Exponents count factors and correspond to square and cubic geometric measurements.

lessons.sourceTitle: Open Up Resources 6–8 Math / IM 6–8 Math

translations.title: Surface Area of a Cube
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will justify the formula for the surface area of a cube using six equal square faces.
A cube has six square faces, each with side length s. One face has area s × s = s², so the entire outside surface has area 6s². This is different from the cube's volume s³. Check that the coefficient six counts faces and the exponent two counts the number of length factors in one face.
Source activity extension: Draw a labeled net of six equal square faces for a cube of edge 5 inches, a different cube of edge 17 units, then generalize to edge s. For each model show one face's area, total surface area 6s², and volume s³. The net must actually fold to a cube; a table of six square areas alone cannot verify a learner-drawn net.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Every face of a cube has square area s².
- A cube has six exposed square faces, giving surface area 6s².
- The cube's volume is s³, a different attribute with cubic units.
- Repeated addition of six equal face areas equals multiplication by 6.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — Cube area: A cube has side length 3 cm. Each face has area 3² = 9 cm², and total surface area is 6 × 9 = 54 cm².
Example 2 — Compare measurements: A cube has side 4 m. Its surface area is 6 × 4² = 96 m², while its volume is 4³ = 64 m³. These numbers cannot be compared as if they measured the same quantity.
Student check: Explain why six faces of area 9 cm² give 54 cm² rather than 27 cm².
Example 3 — Source-sized cube nets: Description: Draw six connected congruent squares in a valid foldable cube net and label every edge. For a 5-inch cube, each square has area 25 in², total outside area 6×25=150 in², and volume 5³=125 in³. For a 17-unit cube, one face has 17²=289 square units; surface area is 6×289=1734 square units and volume 17³=4913 cubic units. A cube of unknown edge s follows 6s² for area and s³ for volume. A teacher inspects correct net connectivity and labels.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Identify the edge length s of the cube.
Step 2: Compute one square face's area s × s = s².
Step 3: Count six exposed equal faces and multiply that one-face area by six.
Step 4: Write the surface area as 6s², in square units.
Step 5: Distinguish it from s³ volume, and check that every face is counted once.
translations.commonMistakes: Multiplying 6 × s × 2 instead of 6 × s² misreads exponents. Using s³ to find outside covering calculates volume, not surface area. Six adjacent squares arranged in any arbitrary pattern do not necessarily fold into a cube. A face area of 25 in² must not be reported as the volume, which is 125 in³ for edge length 5 inches.
translations.quickSummary: The cube surface-area formula 6s² comes from six square faces of area s² each. Cube volume is s³ and uses cubic units.

lessons.sourceTitle: Open Up Resources 6–8 Math / IM 6–8 Math

translations.title: Designing a Tent
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will design a tent for up to four campers, including a floor, and justify its fabric estimate with geometric measurements.
The original Unit 1 capstone explicitly REQUIRES a tent floor. Choose realistic dimensions for up to four people, sketch every fabric panel, and use area of rectangles and triangles to estimate the total fabric required, including that floor. Discuss tent style, height category, sleeping-bag sizes, slope lengths, entrances and allowances; explain what is measured and what is an assumption. Compare the estimates and trade-offs of several student designs with a partner; no single area answer establishes an acceptable tent. The illustrated first-party model below assumes four 2-by-6-foot sleeping bags in one row and a close-fitting 8-by-6-foot floor, without space for an aisle.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- A valid source-aligned tent design accommodates up to four campers and MUST INCLUDE A FLOOR, even if a simplified example excludes seams or optional entrance cut-outs.
- Sketch and label the floor, all roof and end panels, and exactly which panels are included when estimating fabric.
- For a triangular-prism tent, two sloped rectangles cover the roof sides and two triangles cover the ends; add the rectangular floor as a separate required panel.
- Sloping panel length differs from the vertical height; identify perpendicular heights in triangular areas and state any chosen slope-length assumption.
- Compare multiple floor-inclusive designs and justify comfort, height and material trade-offs through teacher-scored reasoning, not only one numeric total.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — Floor-inclusive four-person triangular-prism tent: Assume four sleeping bags are each 2 ft wide and 6 ft long, arranged side-by-side, with no aisle. The rectangular floor must be at least 8 by 6 ft, so floor area is 48 ft². Choose sitting-height 3 ft and tent base width 8 ft; half the triangular end base is 4 ft, giving sloping roof length 5 ft by the 3–4–5 right triangle. Two roof rectangles each 6-by-5 ft use 60 ft² combined. Two triangular ends each have area ½×8×3=12 ft², or 24 ft² total. All required fabric panels, INCLUDING THE FLOOR, use 48+60+24=132 ft² before seams, doors or waste. State explicitly that this snug geometry provides limited headroom and no walkway.
Example 2 — Increase the tent's length for more space: Keep the 8-ft base width, 3-ft height and 5-ft roof slope, but increase length from 6 to 8 ft. Floor area becomes 8×8=64 ft²; two roof panels use 2×8×5=80 ft²; end triangles still use 24 ft². Total required fabric is 64+80+24=168 ft², 36 ft² more than the first model. Compare added floor space with the greater fabric cost and discuss an optional seam allowance separately.
Example 3 — Peer-review a proposed tent: Design an original tent for up to four people using the supplied example specifications, draw and label floor, roof and end panels, and estimate all required areas. Explain why your floor fits the sleeping-bag arrangement, what interior height it provides, and how another design changes the estimate. Teacher review checks dimension consistency, floor inclusion, surface decomposition, assumptions and a defensible comparison.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Review the camper, sleeping-bag and tent-height requirements; choose a realistic layout for up to four people.
Step 2: Sketch a three-dimensional tent and net or labeled panel list, including a mandatory floor, roof sides and both ends.
Step 3: Determine base, length, perpendicular height and true sloped panel lengths in consistent units.
Step 4: Calculate and add all required fabric panels, explicitly including the floor; document separately any opening, seam or waste allowance.
Step 5: Compare alternatives and communicate the resulting estimate, spatial constraints and assumptions to a peer; request teacher assessment of the original design.
translations.commonMistakes: Omitting the floor directly violates the source task: a 21 m² roof-and-end-only estimate is not an acceptable total for a required floor-inclusive design. Multiplying vertical tent height by roof length instead of the actual sloping width underestimates fabric. Four 2-ft-wide sleeping bags require 8 ft of usable width when laid in one row; a floor too small for the chosen arrangement is not valid. The modeled 8-by-6-foot floor is snug and assumes no walkway. A creative design must be reviewed against comfort, dimensions and explicit assumptions, not a single exact machine-graded area.
translations.quickSummary: Design a tent accommodating up to four people with a REQUIRED floor. Add floor, sloping roof and end-panel areas, justify dimensions/height and compare independently reasoned fabric estimates with teacher review.

lessons.sourceTitle: Open Up Resources 6–8 Math / IM 6–8 Math

translations.title: Introducing Ratios and Ratio Language
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will describe two quantities with precise ratio language, including the order of the quantities.
A ratio compares quantities in a named order. For 9 red counters and 6 blue counters, the ratio of red to blue is 9:6, equivalent to 3:2. The reverse comparison, blue to red, is 6:9 or 2:3. A part-to-whole comparison is different: red to total is 9:15 or 3:5. Use drawings, grouped counters, or an accessible text description to keep the compared quantities clear.
Source task extension: Sort an original class collection into two or three named categories, count each category in a labeled table, then write multiple ratio sentences including reversed order and part-to-whole comparisons. Show an actual collection or a text-accessible diagram and ask a partner to check each statement. For a 24-unit-area rectangle shaded in a 2:1 color ratio, use 16 and 8 equal square units. A different shape with 18 equal square units can use 12 and 6; equivalent color ratios do not mean the areas must be equal.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- A ratio compares quantities in the stated order; a:b means a of the first quantity for every b of the second.
- Ratios can be simplified by dividing both counts by the same nonzero number.
- Part-to-part and part-to-whole ratios are different comparisons.
- Represent the groups physically, with labeled diagrams, or with complete sentences.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — Counters: A set contains nine red counters and six blue counters. The red-to-blue ratio is 9:6 = 3:2; the blue-to-red ratio is 6:9 = 2:3. Explain why the two ratios do not mean the same thing.
Example 2 — Whole collection: The same set has 15 counters in total, so the red-to-total ratio is 9:15 = 3:5. Three out of five is the part-to-whole comparison, not the red-to-blue ratio.
Student check: Arrange 8 circles and 12 triangles into equal groups. State triangles-to-circles and circles-to-total ratios.
Example 3 — Sort and shade collections: A labeled set has 6 squares, 3 triangles and 3 circles. Squares:triangles = 6:3 = 2:1, triangles:circles = 3:3 = 1:1, and squares:total = 6:12 = 1:2. Independently color a 24-square-unit rectangle with 16 yellow and 8 blue square units, then create a different shape of area 18 using 12 yellow and 6 blue units. Both display color ratio 2:1, but their total areas differ. Teacher checks actual labels, diagrams, shape correctness and justified ratios.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Identify the two quantities and their units or categories.
Step 2: Read the requested order of comparison.
Step 3: Count the quantities and write a:b in the correct order.
Step 4: If simplifying, divide both terms by the same positive common factor.
Step 5: Read the ratio aloud in context and confirm whether it is part-to-part or part-to-whole.
translations.commonMistakes: Reversing the order of a ratio changes what it means. Do not use the whole total in place of one part unless the problem explicitly requests a part-to-whole ratio. Equal color ratios do not require equal total areas; 16:8 and 12:6 both simplify to 2:1 although one uses 24 and the other 18 square units.
translations.quickSummary: A ratio compares two named quantities in a defined order. Use counters or grouped diagrams to distinguish part-to-part from part-to-whole comparisons.

lessons.sourceTitle: Open Up Resources 6–8 Math / IM 6–8 Math

translations.title: Representing Ratios with Diagrams
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will represent a ratio using labeled collections and accurate sentences.
Six squares and four circles form a labeled collection. A discrete diagram may group shapes by category, while a ratio sentence specifies the order and the group counts. Describe the same collection in words, symbols and a text-accessible list without confusing part-to-part with part-to-whole comparisons.
Source task extension: A ratio diagram may compare unlike units, such as cups of white paint to tablespoons of blue paint: 2 cups white and 6 tablespoons blue gives 2:6 or one cup per three tablespoons. Do not silently convert unlike units into identical units. Source card-sort work also involves three different ingredients in one recipe, where circle, square and triangle symbols represent different quantities/units, and several valid ratio sentences may describe one diagram.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- A discrete diagram records each labeled object or equal unit rather than only writing a numerical answer.
- The order in a ratio matters: squares to circles 6:4 differs from circles to squares 4:6.
- A correct sentence names the categories and quantities represented in the diagram.
- In a discrete snap-cube diagram or measurement context, identify each quantity and its unit before interpreting the ordered ratio. Two cups of white paint to six tablespoons of blue paint does not mean both numbers count the same unit.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: Draw or describe six square tiles and four circle tiles. The squares-to-circles ratio is 6:4 or 3:2; for every 3 squares there are 2 circles.
Example 2: The same collection has 10 tiles, so squares-to-all is 6:10 or 3:5, not 6:4.
Source-aligned diagram dialogue — Represent 2 cups of white paint and 6 tablespoons of blue paint using two separate labeled groups, then compare the statements 'white cups to blue tablespoons is 2:6' and 'one cup white for every three tablespoons blue'. Both encode the same ordered comparison. Have a partner write another valid sentence from your diagram and discuss any disagreement; the diagram and verbal explanation require teacher review.
Example 3 — Three-ingredient recipe card sort: An independently created sauce diagram uses 4 circles for four cups tomato sauce, 2 squares for two tablespoons oil and 1 triangle for one teaspoon oregano. Tomato cups:oil tablespoons = 4:2 = 2:1, oil tablespoons:oregano teaspoons = 2:1, and the complete three-way ratio is 4:2:1 in the stated order. Trade diagrams with a partner and compare three distinct valid descriptions; a teacher evaluates mismatched labels, quantities and disagreements. Warm-up check: 24 ÷ 4 = (1/4)×24 = 6.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Name and count both categories in the collection.
Step 2: Write a labeled list or picture with one mark per unit.
Step 3: Put the requested category first in the ratio.
Step 4: Check the resulting symbolic ratio against the drawn groups.
Step 5: Translate the ratio into a full sentence and distinguish comparisons with the whole.
translations.commonMistakes: Changing the order of the categories reverses the meaning of a ratio. A drawing with unequal or missing units cannot justify the stated counts. Equal ratio numbers in different ordered ingredient comparisons may represent different physical units. A student-created diagram must state which shape and unit represents each ingredient.
translations.quickSummary: Use a discrete diagram or labeled list to justify a ratio sentence. Part-to-part and part-to-whole comparisons must be distinguished.

lessons.sourceTitle: Open Up Resources 6–8 Math / IM 6–8 Math

translations.title: Recipes
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will scale a recipe by multiplying every ingredient by the same factor.
A recipe expresses a ratio of ingredients: if a drink uses 2 measures of powder for every 5 measures of water, doubling the batch requires 4 measures of powder and 10 of water. The resulting ratio stays equivalent because both ingredient amounts changed by the same positive factor. Label ingredient units and use grouped diagrams to justify the scaling.
Source task extension: A cookie recipe uses 5 cups flour per 2 teaspoons vanilla: two batches use 10 cups and 4 teaspoons, three batches use 15 and 6, and five batches use 25 and 10. Drinks with different ingredient proportions may taste different; the order of ingredients and their units matter. For comparisons of sodium concentration, use consistent sodium per equal volume and state the nutritional label values used in any model.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Equivalent recipe ratios multiply each ingredient by the same positive scale factor.
- A diagram with repeated equal batches represents the multiplicative relationship.
- Changing only one ingredient changes the ratio and may change the mixture.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: One batch uses 2 scoops of mix and 5 cups of water. Three batches use 6 scoops and 15 cups; 2:5 = 6:15.
Example 2: Two recipes use mix-to-water ratios 2:5 and 4:8. The ratios are not equivalent because doubling 2 gives 4 but doubling 5 gives 10, not 8.
Example 3 — Cookie batches and saltiness: One batch of cookies needs 5 cups flour and 2 teaspoons vanilla. Two, three and five batches respectively require (10,4), (15,6), and (25,10), all equivalent flour-to-vanilla ratios. For an independently stated drink comparison, Drink A has 200 mg sodium per 500 mL and Drink B has 150 mg per 300 mL. A's rate is 0.4 mg/mL and B's is 0.5 mg/mL, so B is saltier under the model. Teacher reviews diagram, source label interpretation and the original student explanation.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Identify the two ingredient quantities and their physical units.
Step 2: Draw or describe one complete recipe batch as one group.
Step 3: Choose how many identical batches are required.
Step 4: Multiply both ingredient quantities by that same factor.
Step 5: Check equivalence by simplifying the new ingredient ratio.
translations.commonMistakes: Multiplying just the water or just the concentrate does not preserve the recipe. A larger batch must scale both quantities consistently. A bigger sodium count is not sufficient to decide which drink is saltier when container volumes differ; compare a consistent mass-per-volume unit.
translations.quickSummary: Recipe batches represent equivalent ratios when every ingredient quantity is multiplied by the same positive number.

lessons.sourceTitle: Open Up Resources 6–8 Math / IM 6–8 Math

translations.title: Color Mixtures
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will compare color mixture ratios to decide whether two mixtures have the same ingredient proportions.
A color mixture can be modeled by the ratio of blue to yellow liquid. If one batch has 5 mL blue and 15 mL yellow, two identical batches have 10 mL blue and 30 mL yellow. The ratios 5:15 and 10:30 are equivalent; a different blue-to-yellow proportion cannot be assumed to make the same shade. Equal mixing conditions are part of the model.
Historical source task: Build the original 5 mL blue plus 15 mL yellow mixture, evaluate which changes retain its 1:3 blue-to-yellow proportion, and model an unequal addition that can be repaired. Adding 20 mL of each color changes the ratio to 25:35, whereas multiplying each original quantity by the same positive factor preserves shade. Discuss why this proportionality predicts color only under consistent paint properties and mixing conditions.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Mixture ratios compare quantities of the same physical units in a stated order.
- Equivalent mixtures multiply every ingredient quantity by a common scale factor.
- Predict proportional shade equivalence from ratios rather than total liquid amount.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: Mixture A combines 5 mL blue with 15 mL yellow, while B uses 10 mL blue and 30 mL yellow. Since both quantities double, A and B have the same blue-to-yellow proportion 1:3.
Example 2: Mixture C uses 10 mL blue and 20 mL yellow, giving 1:2. This is not equivalent to 1:3 even though the total amounts may look similar.
Example 3 — Repair an altered color mixture: Start with 5 mL blue and 15 mL yellow (1:3). Add 20 mL of each color; the mixture becomes 25 mL blue and 35 mL yellow (5:7), not 1:3. To return to the original ratio without removing liquid, 25 mL blue requires 75 mL yellow, so add another 40 mL yellow. A new 17 mL blue/13 mL yellow mixture can similarly become 17:51 by adding 38 mL yellow. For a separate 8:3 blue:red recipe, Jada's 24:9 is equivalent but Andre's 16:9 is not. Teacher reviews the mixing representation, assumptions and reasoning.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Label the colors, amounts and units for both mixtures.
Step 2: Write blue-to-yellow ratios in the same order.
Step 3: Check whether the same nonzero factor scales both ingredients.
Step 4: Explain if the proportions match or differ.
Step 5: Describe assumptions about concentration and mixing before interpreting the visual shade.
translations.commonMistakes: The ratio 5:15 does not become 10:20 when ingredients are doubled. Comparing only the total liquid amount does not establish equivalent mixtures.
