For any positive count b and cost c, doubling both yields (2c)/(2b)=c/b. Teacher reviews the algebraic and verbal explanation; an isolated number does not prove the generalization.
Example 4: Fill a production table in both directions — At 6 bracelets per hour, 2, 5, and 7 hours yield 12, 30, and 42 bracelets, respectively; 66 bracelets take 11 hours and 100 bracelets take 100/6 = 16 2/3 hours. In an applesauce model, 4 pounds apples make 6 cups; 7 pounds produce 10.5 cups and 10 pounds produce 15 cups, while 9 cups require 6 pounds and 20 cups require 40/3 pounds. Each inverse calculation divides by the correct unit rate and keeps the table quantities aligned.
Example 5: Two simultaneous flows — If a first hose fills 5 gallons in 2 minutes and a second fills 10 gallons in 8 minutes, the constant separate rates are 2.5 and 1.25 gallons/minute. Working simultaneously at those rates, the combined flow is 3.75 gallons/minute and an initially empty 750-gallon pool requires 200 minutes, neglecting leaks and flow changes. Similarly, two eaters consuming 2 and 3 scoops in 5 minutes together finish one scoop per minute under the same-rate assumption. These optional challenges demand explicit assumptions.
Description: Ratio table. The first column is labeled "hours" with values 2, 5, 7, 11, 16.6667; the second column is labeled "bracelets" with values 12, 30, 42, 66, 100; the third column is labeled "bracelets per hour" with value 6 in every row. The displayed 16.6667 is rounded; retain the exact 50/3 hours for computation.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Select a consistent ordering of the two table quantities.
Step 2: Find the rate per one from a known pair.
Step 3: Scale known pairs to missing quantities.
Step 4: Fill each blank using the constant rate.
Step 5: Check every column by dividing matched values.
translations.commonMistakes: Pairs 10:4 and 15:4 are not equivalent because the rates are 2.5 and 3.75. Keeping one entry fixed while scaling the other changes the ratio. A ratio table's columns cannot be scaled independently. When solving for elapsed time from a total, divide by bracelets/hour; when solving for bracelets from time, multiply. A visual 'which one differs' warm-up may permit multiple defensible answers and must be teacher-reviewed.
translations.quickSummary: Equivalent ratio-table columns share a constant unit rate, which can be used to fill and verify all values.

lessons.sourceTitle: Open Up Resources 6–8 Math / IM 6–8 Math

translations.title: More about Constant Speed
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will solve speed and pace problems using rates to predict distance or elapsed time.
Constant speed measures distance traveled per time, while pace describes time per distance. For a known distance and time, find either rate and choose a convenient representation for an unknown. Explain the units and note when the constant-speed assumption is only approximate.
When two people walk toward one another on one trail at constant but possibly unequal speeds, their separation decreases by the SUM of their distances traveled each hour. This is different from tracking a single runner's distance, and the common meeting time must be positive and checked against their starting separation.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Speed = distance ÷ time; pace = time ÷ distance.
- Distance = speed × time and time = distance ÷ speed for nonzero speed.
- Double number lines and ratio tables represent repeated equal distance/time increments.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: A cyclist travels 18 km in 1.5 hours. Speed is 18 ÷ 1.5 = 12 km/h. At that rate 4 hours corresponds to 48 km.
Example 2: A runner moves at 5 m/s. To cover 75 m requires 75 ÷ 5 = 15 seconds; pace is 0.2 second per meter.
Source-task approaching walkers — Two friends begin 24 miles apart and walk toward each other at 3 mi/h and 3.4 mi/h. Their gap closes at 3 + 3.4 = 6.4 miles per hour. After one hour they are 17.6 miles apart; they meet after 24/6.4 = 3.75 hours. If they start at 8:00 a.m., they meet at 11:45 a.m. only under the stated constant-speed/no-stops assumptions. Draw a labeled separation table and discuss rounding.
Example 3: Source walking convergence table — Two walkers begin 24 miles apart at 8:00 a.m. and travel toward each other at 3 and 3.4 miles/hour. A distance-separation table pairs (hours since 8 a.m., miles still apart) as (0,24),(1,17.6),(2,11.2),(3,4.8),(3.75,0). Their combined closing rate is 6.4 miles/hour. They meet at 11:45 a.m. In a second modeled outing they meet after 2.5 hours with one walking 3.4 mph; the jogger's speed is (24/2.5)-3.4 = 6.2 mph. Explain why adding, not subtracting, speeds is correct for walking toward one another.
Example 4: Back on a treadmill — A model 12-mile run in 75 minutes has pace 6.25 minutes per mile and speed 0.16 mile per minute. At the same pace, 8 miles take 50 minutes and in 30 minutes the runner covers 4.8 miles. For opposite-direction motion, one person moves 2 miles in 12 minutes (10 mph) and another moves 1 mile in 24 minutes (2.5 mph): separation increases at 12.5 mph or 5/24 mile per minute, so in 15 minutes they are 3.125 miles apart and after 24 minutes they are 5 miles apart.
Example 5: Constant-speed extension assumptions — If a dog runs 6 mph throughout the walkers' full 3.75-hour meeting interval, its path length is 22.5 miles even though it reverses direction. If the first walker instead moves twice as fast as the second, their 24-mile separation is split in a 2:1 distance ratio, so one travels 16 miles and the other 8 miles. Actual animals may pause or turn, so these are simplified models; students should label the assumption.
Description: Ratio table. The first column is labeled "hours since 8 a.m." and contains 0, 1, 2, 3, 3.75. The second column is labeled "remaining gap miles" and contains 24, 17.6, 11.2, 4.8, 0. Every row reduces the gap by 6.4 miles per hour until meeting. The paired labels form an accessible original alternative to a student drawing.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Identify which quantity is unknown: speed, time, or distance.
Step 2: Find the known rate, preserving compound units.
Step 3: Choose a matching table, diagram or equation.
Step 4: Multiply or divide to solve for the missing quantity.
Step 5: Check the predicted distance/time pair has the same unit rate.
translations.commonMistakes: A speed expressed in km/h cannot be multiplied directly by seconds without converting units. Travel-time estimates require a nonzero rate. Subtracting speeds of walkers who move toward each other underestimates the closing rate. The distance of a reversing dog is path length, not straight-line displacement; mixing these can produce the wrong answer.
translations.quickSummary: Use distance/time unit rates and matching units to solve constant-speed and pace problems.

lessons.sourceTitle: Open Up Resources 6–8 Math / IM 6–8 Math

translations.title: Solving Rate Problems
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will apply unit rates and conversions to solve contextual price and distance problems.
Real-world rates may combine money, distance and time in different units. First convert to shared units, then calculate a rate per one unit. A sensible deal comparison depends on price per equal quantity, not simply the labeled total cost.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Comparable rates use the same underlying measurement units.
- A rate per one unit can scale up or down through equivalent ratios.
- Include conversion factors explicitly in calculations.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: A runner covers 1.5 km in 6 minutes. Since 1.5 km = 1,500 meters, the rate is 250 meters per minute.
Example 2: A 2-liter container costs $3.80 and a 500-mL container costs $1.20. The large container costs $1.90/L; the smaller costs $2.40/L. The large container is cheaper per liter.
Example 3: A hundred-square visual task — On an original text-described 10-by-10 grid, a 5-by-5 shaded corner contains 25 of 100 squares (one quarter), one full column contains 10 of 100 (one tenth), and five full columns plus half of each of five further columns contains 75 of 100 (three quarters). Ask the learner to justify the chosen decomposition, not just report a percent. The original grid photograph or source graphic is not being copied or claimed rendered.
Example 4: Fictional sprint comparison with common units — Under the published one-minute distance data, convert 1,408 yards to 1,287.4752 m; 1 mile to 1,609.344 m; 49,632 inches to 1,260.6528 m; 1,073 m stays 1,073 m; 1.15 km to 1,150 m; and 3,773 feet to 1,150.0104 m, using exact inch/foot/yard metric definitions. Descending modeled distances: antelope, cougar, hare, coyote, ostrich, kangaroo. The coyote and ostrich differ by only 0.0104 m and may appear tied if rounded to the nearest whole meter: preserve precision before ranking and explain assumptions. These are classroom fictional sprint results, not real zoological records.
Example 5: Teacher-assessed offer-card reasoning — When a merchant offers 6 identical 300-mL drinks for $5.40, the modeled rate is $0.90 per drink and $0.003 per mL. An alternative 4 identical 300-mL drinks for $3.80 is $0.95 per drink. Students may create and defend a nearby deceptive offer using their own quantities and explain to a partner why its unit rate is greater or smaller. Original partner cards A–F are not reproduced; persuasive justification and revision require teacher review.
Description: Ratio table. The first column is labeled "fictional competitor" and includes antelope, cougar, hare, coyote, ostrich, kangaroo. The second column is labeled "meters in one minute" and includes 1609.344, 1287.4752, 1260.6528, 1150.0104, 1150, 1073 in descending order. The narrow coyote versus ostrich difference should not be erased by early rounding.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Read the quantities and units in each context.
Step 2: Convert to common measurement units.
Step 3: Compute the desired unit rate using division.
Step 4: Scale or compare the resulting rates.
Step 5: State a conclusion with correct units and reasonableness check.
translations.commonMistakes: Comparing $3.80 with $1.20 without accounting for container size gives an invalid best-value conclusion. Rounding animal distances before deciding ranks can reverse or erase a 0.0104-meter distinction. Unavailable partner-card offer data must never be invented as an authentic publisher card; a first-party example cannot replace the teacher activity.
translations.quickSummary: Convert measurements first, then use rates with matching units for contextual decisions.

translations.title: What Are Percentages?
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will interpret percentages as quantities per 100.
Percent means per hundred. A rate of 35% means 35 out of each 100 equal units, equal to the fraction 35/100 and decimal 0.35. Percentages compare a part to a specified whole, so always state what counts as 100%.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- p% is the ratio p:100, written p/100.
- The whole quantity corresponds to 100%, and zero corresponds to 0%.
- Percent and fraction descriptions must refer to the same whole.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: Twenty-five cents of a dollar is 25/100 = 25%; half a dollar is 50% of a dollar.
Example 2: A class with 12 of 30 learners choosing a topic has 12/30 = 40/100 = 40%, because 30 learners is the 100% whole.
Example 3: Coins as rates per hundred — A penny, nickel, dime, quarter, half-dollar and dollar coin are worth 1, 5, 10, 25, 50 and 100 cents. Relative to a $1 = 100-cent reference, they represent 1%, 5%, 10%, 25%, 50% and 100%. Six dimes total 60 cents = 60% and six quarters total 150 cents = 150%; a percent may exceed 100% when comparing amounts. State which whole the percent refers to.
Example 4: Coins and labeled comparison number line — If one whole dollar is 100%, then 75 cents is $0.75 or 75%, 150 cents is $1.50 or 150%, and three quarters plus five dimes total 125 cents or 125%. To model 120%, one invented valid combination is one dollar coin plus two dimes, and another disjoint-by-coin-type combination is four quarters plus four nickels. Confirm every total in cents, not the number of coins.
Description: Double number line. The top number line is labeled "dollars" and numbers 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.25, 1.5 are indicated. The bottom number line is labeled "percent of one dollar" and numbers 0, 25, 50, 75, 100, 125, 150 are indicated. Corresponding marks refer to the same coin value, even beyond 100%. This description is not a copy of the original coin images.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Identify the whole quantity considered 100%.
Step 2: Identify the measured part of that whole.
Step 3: Make a fraction part/whole.
Step 4: Convert to an equivalent fraction with denominator 100 or multiply by 100%.
Step 5: Interpret the percentage in the original context.
translations.commonMistakes: Claiming 25% means 25 students without specifying the total ignores that the whole may not be 100 students. Assuming every percentage must be at most 100% wrongly excludes six quarters or other amounts above one dollar; distinguishing part of a fixed whole from comparison to a reference is essential.
translations.quickSummary: A percentage states a part relative to a chosen whole of 100 equal percent units.

translations.title: Percentages and Double Number Lines
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will represent percent-of-whole relationships on double number lines.
A double number line can pair a percent scale from 0 to 100% with the corresponding amount scale from 0 to the whole quantity. For 40% of 80, line up 100% with 80 and 50% with 40, then calculate 40% as 32. The number lines must preserve proportional spacing.
Percent scales can extend beyond 100%; 100% identifies the reference quantity, not the maximum possible comparison. If a fundraising goal is $40, then 150% means $60; for an 8-mile reference bike trip, 125% means 10 miles. A double number line must remain proportionally scaled beyond the 100% tick when needed.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- 100% identifies the whole amount, not an unrelated benchmark.
- Corresponding percent/amount pairs are equivalent ratios.
- Matched tick positions on aligned number lines show the same part-to-whole relationship.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: A full tank holds 80 liters. Mark (percent,liters) as (0,0), (25,20), (50,40), (75,60), (100,80). Thus 75% is 60 L.
Example 2: A laptop price is $150, and 20% of it is $30. Paired marks (0%,0), (20%,$30), (100%,$150) explain the proportion.
Source-aligned percentages beyond the whole — A $40 fundraising goal corresponds to 100% = $40, 50% = $20 and 150% = $60. On another double number line, if a Saturday distance of 8 miles is 100%, Sunday at 75% is 6 miles and Monday at 125% is 10 miles. Label both scales past the whole rather than cutting off at the 100% position.
Example 3: Source percent and reference amount — At a $40 fundraising target, 100%, 50% and 150% correspond to $40, $20 and $60, respectively. For a reference Saturday ride of 8 miles, Sunday at 75% is 6 miles and Monday at 125% is 10 miles. These are percent-of-the-Saturday-distance comparisons; use identical percentage intervals on the two aligned scales.
Example 4: Recover the whole from a given part — Under a simplified puppy-growth model, 9 pounds at 20% of eventual weight corresponds to 9/0.20 = 45 pounds, while 9 pounds at 30% corresponds to 9/0.30 = 30 pounds. Identical present weight does not imply identical adult-weight prediction; the percentages name different relative fractions. A different model with 140% of an amount equal to $28 gives a 100% reference of $20. These are ratio exercises, not veterinary predictions.
Example 5: Historical-price ratio only — In a hypothetical classroom comparison of a $0.20 loaf and a $2.50 loaf of the same size, the earlier price is 0.20/2.50 = 8% of the reference price. Applying that same ratio to a modeled $10 hourly wage yields $0.80/hour. This does not claim real historical purchasing power or inflation and requires a clear statement of what is the 100% amount.
Description: Double number line. The top number line is labeled "distance miles" and numbers 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 are indicated. The bottom number line is labeled "percent of Saturday distance" and numbers 0, 25, 50, 75, 100, 125, 150 are indicated. A labeled tick at 125% corresponds to 10 miles; spacing must remain proportional.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Name the whole amount and mark it at 100%.
Step 2: Draw corresponding percent and amount scales beginning at zero.
Step 3: Calculate convenient anchor points, such as 50% or 10%.
Step 4: Use equivalent ratios to fill the target percent or amount.
Step 5: Check the paired values share the same scale factor.
translations.commonMistakes: Placing 80 at 80% when the actual whole is 80 units confuses percent number with amount. Taking 9 × 0.20 instead of 9 ÷ 0.20 when 9 is the part and the unknown is the whole produces a false adult reference. Do not treat comparative historical percentages as verified inflation statistics.
translations.quickSummary: Double number lines connect 0–100% of a specified whole with the corresponding actual quantities.

translations.title: Percentages and Tape Diagrams
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will represent unknown percentages and totals using partitioned tape diagrams.
A tape diagram can divide a whole bar into equal percentage parts. For example, if 25% corresponds to one quarter of the tape, the whole comprises four equal 25% sections. Diagrams can solve either 'what is p% of B?' or 'B is what whole when p% equals C?'.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- A tape diagram's entire bar represents 100% of the chosen whole.
- Equal partitions represent equal fractions of the total amount.
- To recover the whole, divide the known part by its fraction of 100%.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: A 100-seat theater has 25% of seats in one section, so the section has 25 seats. In a four-part tape, each segment represents 25 seats.
Example 2: A quarter of a shipment is 18 boxes. Four equal 25% sections represent 18 × 4 = 72 boxes total.
Source-task inverse percentage puppy — A puppy weighs 9 lb and currently weighs about 20% of its predicted adult weight. A tape split into five equal 20% sections has one section representing 9 lb; the 100% whole is 5×9 = 45 lb. Check 20% of 45 = 9. The weight prediction is an estimate, not a measured claim about every dog.
Example 3: Partitioned source puppy and dog comparisons — In a first-party five-section tape, a 9-pound puppy is one equal 20% segment, so the five segments show an approximate 45-pound whole. When a different dog weighs 90 pounds while the puppy weighs 9, its amount is ten puppy-weight units, so the puppy is 1/10 or 10% of the larger dog's weight and the larger dog is 1,000% of the puppy's weight. Do not swap the 100% reference between comparisons without telling the learner.
Example 4: Two comparative amounts with a $5 whole — A model $5 reference is 100%. At 40% of that reference a learner has $2, which is 2/5 of the original amount. At 150% the other learner has $7.50, which is 3/2 of the original. A tape for 150% can show three equal segments of $2.50 each, where two segments make the $5 reference. Compare the two choices and justify why over 100% is possible in this comparison.
Example 5: Hiking water and a finite supply — If 1.5 liters drunk is 50% of carried water, the full amount was 3 liters; 80% corresponds to 2.4 liters. Bringing 150% of the original 3 liters on a later hike is possible (4.5 liters), but consuming 150% of a fixed 3-liter supply is not possible without refilling or borrowing extra water. Teacher reviews the context claim in addition to the computation.
Description: Tape diagram. One horizontal bar represents 100% of an estimated 45-pound whole and is partitioned into five equal sections, each labeled 20% and 9 pounds. A separate bar represents $5 at 100% with two equal $2.50 sections; three of those sections represents $7.50 at 150%. This is a first-party text alternative; actual accessible diagram rendering remains unverified.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Draw or describe one bar representing the entire 100% whole.
Step 2: Partition the bar into useful equal percentage units.
Step 3: Label each section with its percentage and matching amount.
Step 4: Multiply to find a part, or divide to recover the whole.
Step 5: Check that all sections total 100% and the original full amount.
translations.commonMistakes: Treating a 25% segment as 25 actual items when the whole is unknown confuses percentages with counts. Treating the 9-pound puppy as 20% of every compared dog's weight changes the whole silently. A percent greater than 100% is possible for a comparison, but not for drinking more liquid than a fixed, unreplenished supply.
translations.quickSummary: Percentage tape diagrams show how equal parts sum to the 100% whole and help solve forward or inverse percent problems.

translations.title: Benchmark Percentages
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will calculate benchmark percentages using equivalent simple fractions.
Common benchmark percentages can be calculated without a calculator by relating them to familiar fractions: 10% = one tenth, 25% = one quarter, 50% = one half, and 75% = three quarters. Use partitioned diagrams or decimal equivalences to justify the calculation.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- 10% of a number is one tenth of that number.
- 25% and 75% correspond to one quarter and three quarters.
- 50% means one half, always relative to the stated whole.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: For 120 people, 10% = 12, 25% = 30, 50% = 60, and 75% = 90 people.
Example 2: For an $80 purchase, 25% is $20 and 75% is $60. Check that the two complementary percentages sum to $80.
Example 3: Benchmark percent across different units — From a common reference of 10 liters, 2,000 kilometers or 24 hours, 50% gives 5 L, 1,000 km or 12 h; 10% gives 1 L, 200 km or 2.4 h; 75% gives 7.5 L, 1,500 km or 18 h. Percent is unit-free but the answer must carry the unit of the original quantity. Use halves, tenths and three quarters to explain the operation.
Example 4: Recover the 100% amount from nine — If 9 is 50% of an amount, the amount is 18; if 25%, 36; if 10%, 90; if 75%, 12; if 150%, 6. For each question compute 9 divided by the percent written as a decimal. Do not multiply 9 by 0.75 when 9 is the part already known.
Example 5: Match a ratio to a percentage — Of the first-party pairs (7,14),(5,20),(3,30),(6,8),(20,5), the first values are 50%, 25%, 10%, 75%, 400% of their second values. An unmatched 4% option is intentionally left over. A contextual question about current world age demographics has no supplied dated population or count, so a teacher must provide and cite data rather than accept invented numbers.
Description: Tape diagram. Three separate labeled first-party bars show 1 of 10 equal pieces shaded as 10%, 1 of 2 shaded as 50%, and 3 of 4 shaded as 75%. Each complete bar is the same 100% reference, not a literal count of 100 objects.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Identify which benchmark percentage is needed.
Step 2: Replace it with a known fraction of the whole.
Step 3: Divide the whole into the fraction's equal parts.
Step 4: Multiply by the numerator if needed.
Step 5: Check complementary percentages and correct units.
translations.commonMistakes: 75% is three quarters, not three fourths of a 75-item absolute amount unless the whole is specified. 9 is 75% of an unknown is an inverse-percent question (the whole is 12), not 75% of 9. A current-world-population task needs a dated evidence source, not a fabricated up-to-date number.
translations.quickSummary: Benchmark percentages correspond to simple fractions and can be found by equal partitioning.

lessons.sourceTitle: Open Up Resources 6–8 Math / IM 6–8 Math

translations.title: Solving Percentage Problems
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will select a diagram or table and determine missing information in percent problems.
Percent problems compare a part with a specified whole. A table, tape diagram, or double number line can show the proportional relationship. Some questions omit the whole or the part; identify and request the needed information rather than assuming that 100% means 100 physical objects.
Coupon questions often provide a full price, a discount or an amount already paid. Identify the true reference in each case and distinguish the discount percentage from the final price percentage. An information-gap partner activity is not equivalent to automatically assigning one missing number to every learner.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Every percent calculation needs a clearly defined whole.
- Tape diagrams show partitioned parts, while tables and double lines show equivalent percent/amount pairs.
- Ask for a missing whole or part before computing a meaningful result.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: A class collected $240 and used 30% for books. A tape diagram shows the book amount as 0.30 × 240 = $72.
Example 2: A library says 40% of its books are fiction but does not give a total count. You cannot calculate the number of fiction books until the total book count is known.
Source-specific coupon inverse comparison — A $15 item discounted by 10% saves $1.50 and costs $13.50. A $24 item with a $6 saving has a 6/24 = 25% discount. If one customer pays 80% of another customer's amount for the same item, the full-price payer pays 1/0.8 = 1.25, or 125%, of the discounted amount. That is 25% more relative to the discounted payment, even though the cheaper buyer received a 20% discount relative to full price. Explain the changing reference whole.
Example 3: Percent coupons with changing reference — A $15 full-price product with a 10% discount saves $1.50 and costs $13.50. Saving $6 on a $24 original price is 25% off. If a buyer pays 80% of the original price, the full-price amount is 125% of that buyer's payment; a 20% discount is NOT the same as a 20% markup when the base changes. Discuss which amount each 100% labels.
Example 4: First-party information-gap procedure — A hypothetical sealed problem card asks for a sale amount; the partner's first-party data card contains a $60 full price and a 20% discount. The solver must ASK for the full price and discount, receive those data, justify why each is needed, and calculate $12 saved and $48 paid. No original publisher Music Devices cards or hidden answers are claimed available; the authentic partner exchange, access and teacher observation cannot be replaced by one automatically marked number.
Example 5: Percent from a known fraction — A 36-liter container holding 9 liters is 9/36 = 1/4 = 25% full. An accessible table can pair (liters, percent)=(0,0),(9,25),(18,50),(27,75),(36,100). This is a fresh first-party table and does not certify original task image presentation.
Description: Double number line. The top number line is labeled "liters" and numbers 0, 9, 18, 27, 36 are indicated. The bottom number line is labeled "percent of 36-liter capacity" and numbers 0, 25, 50, 75, 100 are indicated. Equal tick spacing reflects the same capacity reference.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Identify the percent, known amount and unknown amount.
Step 2: Decide what represents 100% and whether it is supplied.
Step 3: Ask for the missing measurement if necessary.
Step 4: Build a matching tape, table, or double number line.
Step 5: Solve using equivalent ratios and verify the percentage of the same whole.
translations.commonMistakes: A percent may be known while the absolute total is unknown; inventing the total creates an unsupported numerical answer. A 20% discount and a 25% markup are consistent when the markup base is the discounted price. Do not fill in a missing partner-card total before it is actually communicated.
translations.quickSummary: Use the whole as 100% in a correctly labeled diagram and obtain any missing information before solving.

lessons.sourceTitle: Open Up Resources 6–8 Math / IM 6–8 Math

translations.title: Finding This Percent of That
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will calculate an arbitrary percentage of a quantity using a factor over 100.
Any percent A can be expressed as A/100 of a specified whole B. The corresponding amount is (A/100) × B, whether A is a benchmark percent or not. A double number line or bar diagram can justify this multiplication as proportional scaling.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- To find A% of B, multiply B × A/100.
- A percent factor may be written as a fraction or decimal.
- Percent-of-a-whole models must preserve consistent units.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: Find 18% of 250: 250 × 18/100 = 45.
Example 2: Find 7.5% of $80: $80 × 0.075 = $6.00. A 10%-comparison ($8) confirms the result is plausible.
Source-aligned audience sizes — A concert attracts 250 people and sets the 100% reference. A basketball event with 30% as many visitors has 75; a play with 140% has 350; and literacy night with 44% has 110. A percentage over 100% is legitimate and means a count greater than the reference. For original attendance estimates, identify whether observations or assumed percentages are being used.
Example 3: School event attendance with a fixed concert reference — In a hypothetical source-style table, the concert is 250 people (100%). Attendance at another event with 30%, 140%, and 44% of that base is 75, 350, and 110 people, respectively. If 50% of the 350-person play also attended the concert, that represents 175 people, which is 175/250 = 70% of the concert audience; the denominator changes with the reference group.
Example 4: A repeated 80%-of-regular-price rule — At sale factor 0.80, regular prices $1, $4, $10, $55 and $120 become $0.80, $3.20, $8, $44 and $96. Expressions (80/100)×x, (8/10)×x, (4/5)×x and 0.8×x are equivalent for all real x. Expressions (8/100)×x, (4/10)×x, (8/5)×x, 80×x, 8×x and 0.08×x are NOT equivalent in general. Teacher asks learners to explain the algebra, not just select checkboxes.
Example 5: Why the shortcut works — 49% of x is (49/100)×x or 0.49x, 6% is 0.06x and 135% is 1.35x. Multiplying a reference whole by p/100 is an equivalent-ratio calculation, so 135% can legitimately be larger than the reference while a 6% portion is smaller.
Description: Ratio table. The first column is labeled "regular price dollars" with values 1, 4, 10, 55, 120. The second column is labeled "sale price dollars" with values 0.8, 3.2, 8, 44, 96. Every corresponding pair uses 80% of regular price, which can be expressed as four-fifths.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Identify the exact whole B.
Step 2: Rewrite A% as A/100 or A ÷ 100.
Step 3: Multiply the whole by the percent factor.
Step 4: Simplify the result with compatible units.
Step 5: Check a nearby benchmark percentage to confirm reasonableness.
translations.commonMistakes: Multiplying by the raw number 18 instead of 18/100 makes an 18% calculation one hundred times too large. An overlap of 175 play/concert participants is 50% of the play attendance but 70% of the concert attendance, because the reference whole changes. Do not accept 8/100 as equivalent to 80/100.
translations.quickSummary: Calculate A percent of B as (A/100) times B, with a correctly identified whole.

lessons.sourceTitle: Open Up Resources 6–8 Math / IM 6–8 Math

translations.title: Finding the Percentage
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will find what percentage one positive quantity represents of another.
To determine the percentage represented by part C of a positive whole B, divide C by B and multiply by 100%. A percentage may exceed 100% when the part being compared is greater than the reference amount. The denominator must be the reference whole, not the part.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- C is (C/B) × 100% of B, for a nonzero reference B.
- The whole chosen as 100% controls the meaning of a comparison.
- The percentage may exceed 100% in growth or reference comparisons.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: 30 students of a 120-student cohort represent (30 ÷ 120) × 100% = 25%.
Example 2: A quantity grows from 40 to 50. The new quantity is 50/40 × 100% = 125% of the original; the increase is (10/40) × 100% = 25%.
Example 3: Rope percentage table — In a first-party 20-minute benchmark, the table (minutes, decimal of benchmark, percent) pairs (20,1,100%), (15,0.75,75%), (24,1.2,120%), and (9,0.45,45%). Divide the time by 20 before multiplying by 100; the 24-minute result can exceed 100% because the comparison is to a 20-minute reference. Explain why 120% of this time is not 120 minutes.
Example 4: Occupancy ratio with a safety boundary — For a posted maximum of 75 people, 9 people represent 9/75×100 = 12%, 51 people represent 68%, and 84 people represent 112%. Because 84 exceeds the limit by 9 people, 112% is a valid arithmetic comparison but not an allowable occupancy. Never treat 112% capacity as permission to exceed a building's legal maximum; teacher discussion reviews the interpretation.
Example 5: True-or-false proportional claims — One-quarter of 512 is 128 and one-quarter of 500 is 125, so they differ. Ninety percent of 133 equals 0.9×133 = 119.7. Thirty percent of 44 equals 13.2 and three percent of 440 also equals 13.2. Twenty-one out of 28 and thirty out of 40 are both 75%. The teacher may accept different correct arguments rather than a single calculation route.
Example 6: Historical extension assumptions — In a source-stated model with 1,386 million cubic kilometers of water, assume 96% is salt water and 4% is fresh. The corresponding volumes are 1,330.56 and 55.44 million cubic kilometers. These percentages and total are task premises, not freshly verified scientific estimates; 71% of Earth's SURFACE being water is a different measurement from 96% of the water VOLUME being saline.
Description: Ratio table. The first column is labeled "jump-rope time minutes" and values 20, 15, 24, 9 are indicated. The second column is labeled "time divided by 20" with values 1, 0.75, 1.2, 0.45. The third column is labeled "percent of 20 minutes" and values 100, 75, 120, 45 are indicated. Describing the table does not certify the actual student renderer.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Identify the reference whole B and part C.
Step 2: Write C divided by B in the correct order.
Step 3: Multiply the resulting ratio by 100%.
Step 4: State the percent and whether it represents total relative to the base or an increase.
Step 5: Check against simple fractions and the context.
translations.commonMistakes: 50 is 125% of 40, but it represents a 25% increase—not a 125% increase. The reference denominator matters. Percent over 100 can be a valid comparison but must not be confused with legal permission for over-capacity occupancy. Earth's surface fraction and Earth's water-volume fraction use different denominators.
translations.quickSummary: Compute part ÷ reference whole × 100% and distinguish percent-of-base from percent increase.

lessons.sourceTitle: Open Up Resources 6–8 Math / IM 6–8 Math

translations.title: Painting a Room
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will use rates, unit conversions and percentages to build a justified painting-project estimate.
A room-painting task requires dimensional measurements, conversion of surface area to paint coverage, material prices, labor rates and reasonable assumptions. Subtract doors or windows only when explicitly excluded, specify how many coats are needed, and present costs and time with units. Different reasonable dimensions or efficiency assumptions lead to different defensible answers.
A historical room-painting activity includes different lengths in yards and feet, openings such as windows, doors and mirrored closet sections, and cost/time assumptions. Convert before calculating and trace the original floor-plan geometry, interior closet faces and mirrored exclusions explicitly before claiming a complete area. Explicitly distinguish a worked outer-wall subtotal from the complete room, which may require inside-closet surfaces and more paint.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Wall area is measured in square units, and paint coverage is square units per volume of paint.
- Use rates for paint consumption and labor time, and percentages for contingencies.
- Explicit assumptions about openings, coats and waste require teacher review.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: A 4 m × 3 m room has 2.5 m-high walls. Wall area is perimeter × height = 2(4+3) × 2.5 = 35 m². With two coats and no deducted openings, the coverage task is 70 m².
Example 2: If paint covers 10 m² per liter per coat, 70 m² requires 7 L. At $12/L, paint costs $84; adding a 10% supply allowance yields $92.40 before rounding to purchase container sizes.
Source-aligned partial room budget — In a simplified rectangular bedroom, side lengths are 3 yards (9 ft) and 10 ft and wall height is ASSUMED to be 8 ft. The four OUTER walls have area 2(9+10)×8 = 304 ft². A 5-by-3 ft window and a 7-by-3 ft door are excluded, leaving 304−15−21 = 268 ft² of exposed outer wall. This is NOT the complete area for a room with an interior closet: the source floor plan, inside-closet surfaces, small 0.5-ft-wide partition and mirrored-door exclusions must be analyzed before treating this rectangular outer-wall estimate as complete. At an assumed coverage of 350 ft² per gallon per coat, the outer-wall subtotal requires 268/350 ≈ 0.766 gallons for one coat before waste or package rounding. Teacher reviews the measurements, missing data, rates and reasonableness of the project estimate.
Example 3: Coverage and package choices — The source's advertisement models 2 quarts covering 175 square feet for ONE coat, or 87.5 square feet per quart per coat. For a verified paintable wall area A square feet and two coats, the paint requirement is (2A/175)×2 = 4A/175 quarts before whole-container rounding. The teacher's discussion gives 7 one-quart cans, 2 one-gallon cans, or 1 gallon plus 3 quarts as candidate purchase combinations for the complete source room. These are examples, not an independently checked exact figure-based wall-area proof. Seven quarts cover at most 7×87.5/2 = 306.25 square feet for two coats.
Example 4: Coupon and purchasing alternatives — Before any supplies, seven one-quart cans at $10.90 each cost $76.30; two one-gallon cans at $34.90 cost $69.80; one gallon and three quarts cost $34.90 + 3×$10.90 = $67.60. A coupon taking 20% off only the one-quart cans makes each quart $8.72, so seven quarts cost $61.04 and one gallon plus three discounted quarts costs $61.06. These are candidate package prices IF they cover the verified project: choices of wasted paint, purchase quantities and unpriced tools mean there is not a unique total supplies cost. A 5-gallon can at $165 is another offered package, often far more paint than this task needs.
Example 5: Wall-face area and labor rate — The east wall is 3 yards = 9 feet long and 8 feet high, so its full face is 72 square feet. A 5×3-ft south-window opening removes 15 square feet and a 7×3-ft west-door opening removes 21 square feet. The teacher explicitly warns to include the 3 square feet above the door and the 0.5-ft-wide partition's exposed 0.5×8 = 4-square-foot end face, as well as other partition faces. Painting the east face with two coats took 96 minutes; if a validated complete paintable area were A, a constant solo productivity model predicts 96×A/72 minutes total, not 96 divided by a guessed 25%. If two people then take 150 minutes for the remaining work, the model savings are 96×(A−72)/72−150 minutes. Supply the actual validated A and state how the second worker's productivity is modeled before asserting a unique time saved.
Description: Ratio table. The first column is labeled "candidate paint purchase" with entries "seven 1-quart cans", "two 1-gallon cans", and "one 1-gallon plus three 1-quart cans". The second column is labeled "paint quantity in quarts" with values 7, 8 and 7. The third column is labeled "paint price before coupon in dollars" with values 76.30, 69.80 and 67.60; the fourth column is labeled "paint price with coupon on quart cans only in dollars" with values 61.04, 69.80 and 61.06. This text table is not a substitute for the original geometric floor plan or a quote for missing equipment.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Draw or list the room walls and their dimensions.
Step 2: Compute wall area and account for openings and number of coats.
Step 3: Use a paint-coverage rate to estimate required liters.
Step 4: Apply unit prices, labor rates and any explicitly justified contingency.
Step 5: Check assumptions, units and rounding; present a teacher-reviewable estimate.
translations.commonMistakes: Confusing square meters with cubic meters or forgetting a second coat understates paint requirements. One fixed numerical estimate cannot assess an open-ended design rationale. Do not price only the paint as the entire supply budget. Under the source, a two-coat job doubles one-coat coverage demand; area for the east face does not establish completion percentage of all paintable wall faces. A 20%-off coupon applies to quart cans, not gallons.
translations.quickSummary: A painting estimate combines wall areas, coverage rates, costs and uncertainty; justify the model and give units.

lessons.sourceTitle: Open Up Resources 6–8 Math / IM 6–8 Math

translations.title: Size of Divisor and Size of Quotient
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will estimate how changing a positive divisor changes the quotient and explain what the quotient means.
Division can ask how many groups of a given size fit in a quantity. For the same positive dividend, a smaller positive divisor gives more groups, while a larger positive divisor gives fewer. Use familiar whole-number cases first, then fractions and decimals. Dividing by zero is undefined, so this comparison assumes a positive nonzero divisor.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Dividend ÷ divisor = quotient; interpret the result as a number of equal groups or an amount per group.
- With a fixed positive dividend, dividing by a smaller positive number gives a larger quotient.
- Predict whether the answer is greater or smaller than 1 before computing.
- Division by 0 is undefined.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 — One dividend, three divisors: 12 ÷ 3 = 4, 12 ÷ 0.5 = 24, and 12 ÷ 24 = 0.5. Interpret each as how many groups of the indicated size fit into 12.
Example 2 — Compare without calculation: Is 8 ÷ 0.25 larger or smaller than 8? A group of size 0.25 is smaller than one whole, so more than eight such groups fit into 8; the exact quotient is 32.
Source-task stack investigation: A stack 72 inches tall with books 2 inches thick has 72÷2=36 books. A 43-inch stack of half-inch books contains 43÷(1/2)=86 books. Predict how the quotient changes as positive divisor size decreases. For fixed dividend 5000, compare 5000÷5=1000 and 5000÷500000=0.01.
Example 3: Predict four mental quotients — Keeping dividend 5,000 fixed, 5,000÷5 = 1,000; 5,000÷2,500 = 2; 5,000÷10,000 = 0.5; and 5,000÷500,000 = 0.01. Before calculating, predict that each larger positive divisor reduces the quotient; dividing by a divisor greater than the dividend produces a number below 1.
Example 4: Stack height as a quotient — A 5-foot stack is 60 inches tall, but photographs of bricks, boxes, notebooks and coins do NOT supply a unique thickness. Measure or estimate actual item height before dividing 60 inches by item thickness; a source photo is not a measurement record. For known thicknesses, 72-inch stack / 2-inch books = 36 books, and 43-inch stack / 0.5-inch books = 86 books. Draw separate group-count models and explain why the thinner books produce a larger count.
Example 5: Sort by quotient magnitude — Much greater than 1: 30÷0.5=60, 30÷0.45≈66.67 and 18÷0.18=100. Close to 1: 9÷10=0.9, 18÷19≈0.9474 and 15,000÷14,500≈1.03448. Close to 0: 9÷10,000=0.0009 and 15,000÷1,500,000=0.01. Discuss why 'close to' depends on a comparison scale rather than a universal cutoff. Original teacher-supplied sorted cards remain a separate unverified resource.
Example 6: Near-one extension — For a positive fixed dividend of 12, 12÷11.9≈1.00840, 12÷12.1≈0.99174, and 12÷12=1. As divisors approach 12 from below or above, the quotient approaches 1 without necessarily equaling 1. A 12÷0 expression is UNDEFINED, not a large numerical answer.
Description: Ratio table. The first column is labeled "fixed dividend" and values 5000, 5000, 5000, 5000 are indicated. The second column is labeled "positive divisor" and values 5, 2500, 10000, 500000 are indicated. The third column is labeled "quotient" and values 1000, 2, 0.5, 0.01 are indicated. Teacher assessment still must check explanation of pattern.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Identify the dividend and the nonzero divisor.
Step 2: Interpret the division as equal sharing or counting how many groups fit.
Step 3: Estimate whether the quotient will be greater or less than the dividend.
Step 4: Compute the quotient by a suitable model or multiplication check.
Step 5: Explain why the size of the divisor changes the number of groups.
translations.commonMistakes: A smaller positive divisor does not make a smaller quotient when the dividend is fixed and positive. Do not divide by zero, and do not confuse group size with group count. Do not use missing stack-photo dimensions as if they were measured facts; item count is a quotient only after item thickness is known. A quotient close to 1 may be above or below 1.
translations.quickSummary: For a fixed positive total, smaller positive groups mean more groups. Predict quotient size from the divisor before calculating.

lessons.sourceTitle: Open Up Resources 6–8 Math / IM 6–8 Math

translations.title: Meanings of Division
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will interpret division as equal sharing or counting equal groups and connect it to multiplication.
The same expression can model how many groups fit in a total or how much belongs to one group. Division finds a missing factor in a multiplication equation. A labeled tape diagram must show which quantity is the number of groups and which is the group size.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- For nonzero b, a ÷ b = c means b × c = a.
- Group-count and group-size questions can use the same arithmetic with different units.
- Tape diagrams show how total, size per group, and number of groups are related.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: Twelve meters of ribbon are cut into 3-meter pieces: 12 ÷ 3 = 4 pieces, a group-count question.
Example 2: Twelve meters of ribbon are divided equally among 3 people: 12 ÷ 3 = 4 meters per person, a group-size question.
Example 3: Two meanings for 20÷4 — Sharing 20 stickers evenly into 4 groups gives 5 stickers per group (partitive division). Making groups of 4 stickers from 20 gives 5 groups (quotitive division). Both yield 5 but answer different questions and require labels; a teacher can accept different sound verbal contexts.
Example 4: Bags of almonds with fraction groups — A 12-pound stock of almonds put into 6-pound bags requires 12÷6=2 bags; divided evenly into 6 bags each bag gets 12÷6=2 pounds. Similarly, 12÷4=3 can mean 3 bags of 4 pounds OR 3 pounds per bag when sharing into 4 bags. Twelve divided by two gives 6, while 12÷(1/2)=24 half-pound bags. Each statement must specify whether the divisor counts bags or specifies pounds per bag.
Example 5: Why zero is not a valid slice size — A 1-loaf bread cut into half-loaf slices makes 2 equal slices and into one-fifth-loaf slices makes 5. Dividing 1 loaf by zero-loaf slices does not define any positive slice length, so 1÷0 is undefined rather than zero or infinity. Even if smaller positive sizes create arbitrarily many slices, no finite group has size exactly zero.
Description: Tape diagram. A first bar represents 12 pounds partitioned into two equal labeled 6-pound segments, with unknown number of bags 2. A second bar represents the same 12-pound total partitioned into six equal 2-pound segments, with unknown weight per bag 2 pounds. The identical numeric quotient corresponds to two different quantities; actual visual/tactile task completion remains unverified.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: State the total and the requested unknown.
Step 2: Identify whether the unknown is count of groups or size of each group.
Step 3: Draw or describe equal segments of a tape.
Step 4: Write the related multiplication equation.
Step 5: Find and interpret the quotient with appropriate units.
translations.commonMistakes: The number of groups and the amount in one group are different quantities; a bare numeric answer without units can conceal the wrong interpretation. A student who says '2' for 12÷6 but omits whether the answer is bags or pounds has not explained which division interpretation is meant. Zero-sized slices are not legitimate equal parts of a loaf.
translations.quickSummary: Division finds a missing factor. Explain whether the quotient means how many groups or how much in one group.

lessons.sourceTitle: Open Up Resources 6–8 Math / IM 6–8 Math

translations.title: Interpreting Division Situations
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will represent division situations involving fractions with diagrams and matching equations.
Fractional groups can be represented on a number line or tape divided into equal parts. Use the chosen whole consistently and write multiplication or division equations that express the same relationship. The quotient may be a whole number, mixed number or proper fraction.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- A fraction is meaningful only relative to a clearly identified unit whole.
- A ÷ b asks how many b-sized groups fit in A, or the size per group when b is the group count.
- The related equation b × q = A checks the division.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: How many one-quarter-cup portions fit into 1.5 cups? 1.5 ÷ 0.25 = 6 because six quarter-cups make 1.5 cups.
Example 2: A half-liter is shared among 4 people: (1/2) ÷ 4 = 1/8 liter per person. Four eighth-liters reassemble the half-liter.
Source-context homemade jam jars: Four jars each contain 2¼ cups, so the total is 4×2¼=9 cups. Five jars sharing 7½ cups need 1½ cups each; 6¾ cups at ¾ cup per jar fill (27/4)÷(3/4)=9 jars. Draw two labeled diagram types and explain the unknown group size versus unknown group count.
Example 3: First-party complete source jam and granola set — Four jars holding 2 1/4 cups each contain 9 cups total (4×2.25=9). Five equal jars from 7 1/2 cups hold 1.5 cups each (7.5÷5=1.5). A 6 3/4-cup total filled at 3/4 cup per jar makes 9 jars, because 9×(3/4)=27/4. A 26-ounce granola recipe measured using a 4-ounce scoop needs 6 1/2 scoopfuls, or six full scoops plus one half; 14 ounces evenly distributed in 4 bags is 3 1/2 ounces per bag. For each, distinguish missing total, missing unit quantity and missing number of groups.
Example 4: Independent diagram reasoning — A bar labeled 7.5 cups with five equal segments has 1.5 cups per segment, showing the known group count. A different bar labeled 6.75 cups with each 0.75-cup segment has nine such segments, showing the unknown group count. Four jars each holding 2.25 cups use multiplication to find 9 cups. A flashed dot array may be partitioned into different rectangles, but its original image was not checked for a reliable dot count; do not invent one.
Description: Tape diagram. One first-party bar totals 7.5 cups of jam with five equal labeled 1.5-cup jars; a second bar totals 6.75 cups and has nine equal labeled 0.75-cup jars. Each diagram is a text description; the publisher's drag-and-drop fraction-jar applet is not reproduced and its interactive equivalence is not verified.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Identify the whole and divide it into suitable equal parts.
Step 2: Label the total, group size or group count.
Step 3: Represent the quantities on a tape or number line.
Step 4: Write the division and matching multiplication equation.
Step 5: Compute and check using the original units and grouping meaning.
translations.commonMistakes: Changing the meaning of one whole midway invalidates a fraction model. A divisor that represents group size is not the same as the number of people receiving shares. If 26 ounces are measured with a 4-ounce scoop, six FULL scoops alone supply only 24 ounces; the seventh scoop need only be half full. Drawing an original jam bar does not demonstrate actual operable fraction bars in the student interface.
translations.quickSummary: Fraction division can be reasoned about with equal partitions and multiplication equations before applying an algorithm.

lessons.sourceTitle: Open Up Resources 6–8 Math / IM 6–8 Math

translations.title: How Many Groups? (Part 1)
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will count how many unit-fraction groups fit into a quantity using a known whole.
Pattern blocks can represent a whole and equal fractional regions. If a hexagon is one whole and two matching trapezoids cover it, each trapezoid represents one-half. Division by a unit fraction counts the number of such fractional units in the given amount.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- A unit fraction 1/n partitions a whole into n equal areas or lengths.
- Dividing A by 1/n counts n times as many unit-fraction groups as wholes.
- The whole represented by one block must remain fixed.
Historical pattern-block area convention: when one matching regular hexagon represents ONE whole, each small triangle represents 1/6, each rhombus 1/3 and each trapezoid 1/2. These are RELATIVE area units, not intrinsic fractions of any named shape.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: A whole is one regular hexagon. Three equal rhombi form its area, so 1 ÷ (1/3) = 3 rhombus-sized groups.
Example 2: Two wholes contain six 1/3-size portions: 2 ÷ (1/3) = 6. The inverse check is 6 × (1/3) = 2.
Original-style pattern-block tasks: Take the full hexagon as 1 whole. Six triangles or three rhombi or two trapezoids match its area. Thus a hexagon and a trapezoid total 1½ hexagon-wholes. Use labeled piece diagrams to explain why the reference whole matters and ask for teacher review of original student assemblies.
Example 3: First-party complete source pattern-block group counts — Use one matching hexagon as one whole. A triangle is 1/6, a rhombus is 1/3 and a trapezoid is 1/2 of its area; four triangles therefore equal 2/3, three rhombi equal 1, two hexagons equal 2 and one hexagon plus one trapezoid equal 1.5 wholes. Three 1/6 triangles form 1/2 whole and two groups of 3/2 each form 3 wholes. These are AREA equivalents, not universal fractions independent of reference.
Example 4: Quotients with visual partition explanations — Four wholes contain eight 1/2 groups; 2 wholes contain three 2/3 groups; 1.5 wholes contain nine 1/6 groups. Also one whole contains 4/3 groups of size 3/4, because one full 3/4 group leaves 1/4, which is one-third of another 3/4 group. Compare group count versus group size before a student assembles original pattern blocks.
Example 5: Equations for matched groups — Eight 5-dollar bills give 8×5=40, so 40÷5=8 bills; nine one-third portions equal 9×(1/3)=3, so 3÷(1/3)=9. If the full tape is 1 and divided into five equal 1/5 segments, 5×(1/5)=1 and 1÷(1/5)=5. A student must identify what each whole represents to use the pattern-block fractional relationships correctly.
Description: Tape diagram. One labeled unit bar is partitioned into six equal one-sixth pieces; the first two pieces together form a rhombus-sized one-third group, the first three form a trapezoid-sized one-half group, and all six form one hexagon-sized whole. This is an original text model and does not establish accessible actual source pattern-block manipulation.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Label the block or tape that represents exactly one whole.
Step 2: Identify the unit fraction's size as one of n equal parts.
Step 3: Partition each whole into equal parts.
Step 4: Count the unit-fraction groups across all wholes.
Step 5: Check that group count × group size equals the total.
translations.commonMistakes: Counting pieces without fixing the meaning of a whole is invalid: the same shape may represent a different fraction under another convention. Four wholes divided into halves yields eight groups, not two. A trapezoid's meaning is 1/2 only when the hexagon is the designated whole.
translations.quickSummary: Unit-fraction division asks how many equal fractional portions fit within the specified whole or total.

lessons.sourceTitle: Open Up Resources 6–8 Math / IM 6–8 Math

translations.title: How Many Groups? (Part 2)
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will use non-unit fraction groups and pattern-block wholes to find fractional quotients.
Now groups may measure several equal fractional parts of a fixed whole. For example, when a red trapezoid represents the whole, a smaller triangular piece may represent one-third of it. A group of size two-thirds contains two such pieces, so count complete groups and any leftover fraction of a group.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- A non-unit fraction a/b consists of a parts, each of size 1/b of the whole.
- A quotient can be a non-integer number of groups.
- Verify with (number of groups) × (size of group) = given total.
Switching the reference whole changes fractions: if the trapezoid is 1 whole, a small triangle is 1/3, a rhombus is 2/3 and the hexagon is 2 trapezoid-wholes.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: How many 2/3-sized groups fit in 2 wholes? Each whole has three thirds; six thirds divided into pairs gives 3 groups, so 2 ÷ (2/3) = 3.
Example 2: How many 3/4-sized groups fit in 3/2 wholes? The total is 6 quarters and each group is 3 quarters, so there are 2 groups.
Source-specific change of whole: If one trapezoid represents 1 whole, 3 rhombi each 2/3 whole make 3×(2/3)=2 trapezoid-wholes. One hexagon also represents two trapezoid-wholes. With a hexagon as the whole, the same matching rhombus would instead be 1/3; justify by area composition.
Example 3: First-party complete fraction-strip arithmetic — Two divided by 1/2 is 4 groups; three divided by 1/5 is 15; 1 1/4 divided by 1/8 is 10. One divided by 2/6 is 3; two divided by 2/9 is 9; and four divided by 2/10 is 20. Verify each by multiplying the group count by the fractional group size. A preprinted fraction strip of units may not include tenths, so two-tenths can be rewritten as one-fifth.
Example 4: Critique two pattern-block arguments — With one trapezoid as one whole, a triangle is 1/3, a rhombus is 2/3 and a hexagon is 2 wholes. Thus the number of rhombi making a trapezoid is 1 ÷ (2/3) = 1 1/2. After placing one rhombus, the leftover triangle is one-third of the trapezoid but HALF of a rhombus, so adding 1/3 groups to one rhombus uses the wrong denominator. Both ?×(2/3)=1 and 1÷(2/3)=? correctly express the unknown.
Example 5: Physical situations requiring labeled quotient — A 1.5-mile park circuit fits twice into a 3-mile ride. A 3/4-yard ribbon length fits four times into 3 yards, so four gift boxes can each receive one full ribbon length. A hose filling at 1/3 gallon per minute needs six minutes for 2 gallons. A 'heaping teaspoon versus heaping tablespoon' problem lacks a specified standardized mound geometry and cannot be answered uniquely by assuming exactly three heaps.
Description: Tape diagram. One trapezoid whole is divided into three equal triangles; two triangles comprise one rhombus of size 2/3. A bracket over all three triangles equals 1 1/2 rhombus groups, and a label notes that the leftover third is half of the group, not a third of the group. Visual model accuracy and learner drawing/dragging remain unverified.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Fix one whole and divide it into equal fractional parts.
Step 2: Express the total and group size using a common unit fraction.
Step 3: Count how many groups of the specified number of parts fit.
Step 4: Include fractional remainders as portions of a group.
Step 5: Check the result by multiplying by the original divisor.
translations.commonMistakes: Treating every colored pattern block as an entire whole loses the fractional relationships; choose and keep one reference whole. A remainder's fraction of the ORIGINAL whole is not necessarily its fraction of a DIVISOR group. Do not report 1 1/3 rhombi for a trapezoid when the actual group size is 2/3.
translations.quickSummary: Non-unit fraction division groups a given number of equal fractional parts and may produce whole or fractional group counts.

lessons.sourceTitle: Open Up Resources 6–8 Math / IM 6–8 Math

translations.title: Using Diagrams to Find the Number of Groups
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will create and interpret a tape diagram for more than one fractional group.
When the group size is a fraction, partitions of a tape can show how many such groups fit into a quantity. Subdivide the total and group size using a common small fractional unit. A quotient greater than one can be expressed as a mixed number of groups, rather than rounding to a whole group.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- A tape diagram must use equal-length sections for equal fractional units.
- Dividing a fractional total by a fractional group size can yield a mixed-number group count.
- Use multiplication to verify the total.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: A 1.5-meter ribbon is divided into 2/5-meter segments. In tenths, the total is 15/10 and each segment is 4/10, so 15/4 = 3 3/4 groups.
Example 2: There are 5/4 liters of juice, poured in portions of 1/2 liter each. In quarters, five quarters contain 2.5 pairs of quarters, so (5/4) ÷ (1/2) = 5/2 = 2.5.
Source fractional tape model: How many 2/3-sized groups fit in 1? Draw 1 tape divided into three thirds, group two-thirds together, then note that the remaining third is half a 2/3 group: 1÷(2/3)=1½ groups. How many 2½-sized groups fit into 10? Four, because 4×2½=10. Label group size and count.
Example 3: First-party source fraction tape problems — 10 ÷ 2 1/2 = 4 complete groups. Seven divided into groups of size 2 contains 3 1/2 groups; the remaining 1 is 1/2 of a GROUP of 2, not 1/7 of the total. One divided by 2/3 is 3/2 groups, while one divided by 3/4 is 4/3 groups. Three divided by 2/3 is 9/2 groups, and 5 divided by 3/2 is 10/3 groups, or 3 1/3. Include a teacher-graded labeled tape for fractional-group reasoning.
Example 4: Books, mass and inverse unit rate — Six inches divided by 3/8 inch per book gives 16 books. A 2 3/4-pound quantity contains 5 1/2 groups of 1/2 pound. A situation 5 ÷ 1 1/2 = 10/3 can ask how many 1.5-meter lengths fit into a 5-meter ribbon, so 3 whole lengths plus a one-third length are available mathematically (but if only complete cuts are allowed, the answer in complete lengths is 3). Always state whether fractional groups make sense in the context.
Example 5: Reconstruct fraction diagrams from known source quantities — Two kg of flour used at 2/5 kg per recipe make 5 batches, because 5×2/5=2. Three and one-half cups rice at 3/4 cup per serving allow 14/3 = 4 2/3 mathematical servings. Four full 3/4-cup portions use 3 cups, leaving 1/2 cup, which is 2/3 of another full serving. A literal meal-planning answer might require rounding down to four complete portions; mathematical and contextual questions are different.
Description: Tape diagram. An original bar representing 3.5 cups is partitioned into fourteen equal one-quarter-cup sections. Four consecutive groups of three sections represent four complete 3/4-cup servings, leaving two one-quarter sections that are two-thirds of another serving. The text represents exact fraction logic but not a verified responsive diagram editor.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Draw a tape that represents the full total.
Step 2: Mark one group of the given fractional size.
Step 3: Subdivide into a shared small unit to compare sizes.
Step 4: Count whole groups and the fraction of the next group.
Step 5: Check by multiplying the group count and group size.
translations.commonMistakes: Rounding fractional group counts hides that some of the total can remain as part of another group; keep the exact fraction when the context permits. Seven divided by two is 3.5 groups, not 3.5 units per group. A left-over half-cup is two-thirds of a three-quarter-cup portion; preserve the fractional GROUP unit.
translations.quickSummary: Tape partitions make fractional group-count division visible, including non-integer quotients.

lessons.sourceTitle: Open Up Resources 6–8 Math / IM 6–8 Math

translations.title: What Fraction of a Group?
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will interpret a quotient less than one as a fraction of a complete group.
A quotient below 1 means the available total is smaller than the prescribed group size. Ask what fraction of one whole group is present; describe the fraction of a group rather than declaring zero groups. A common-unit tape diagram connects the fraction to a multiplication check.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- If 0 < total < positive group size, the number of groups lies between 0 and 1.
- The quotient describes what fraction of a full group the total represents.
- Use common fractional units to compare the total and the complete group.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: A serving uses 3/4 cup, but 1/2 cup is available. The available amount is (1/2) ÷ (3/4) = 2/3 of a serving because 2/3 × 3/4 = 1/2.
Example 2: A full group is 5/6 meter and only 1/3 meter is available. The fraction of a group is (1/3) ÷ (5/6) = 2/5.
Example 3: First-party source ice-cream batches — A full batch needs 9 cups of milk. Monday 12 cups is 12/9=4/3 batches, Tuesday 22.5 cups is 22.5/9=2.5 batches, Thursday 6 cups is 6/9=2/3 of a batch and Friday 7.5 cups is 7.5/9=5/6 of a batch. The reference unit is nine cups per ONE batch, so zero full batches does not imply zero ice cream.
Example 4: Rope-ratio direction — If a first-party model rope C measures 3 equal grid units and rope D measures 9 units, D is 9/3=3 times C, while C is 3/9=1/3 times D. Both are valid statements for different reference ropes. The publisher's draggable rope applet also has ropes A and B with grid lengths not established in this text; never infer those two lengths without the actual interactive source.
Example 5: Describe part of a reference — Three is one-third of 9; 1/2 is one-tenth of 5. Likewise 2 1/4 of a 3-unit whole is (9/4)÷3=3/4 of the reference. Before finding fractions of ropes or milk batches, write q×(whole)=part or part÷whole=q and label which total is the chosen whole.
Description: Tape diagram. One first-party bar spans nine equal cup segments labeled as one complete 9-cup batch; a second bar spans six of those same cup segments and is labeled two-thirds of a batch; a third extends to 12 segments and is labeled four-thirds of a batch. Source draggable rope interaction and authentic student drawing remain unverified.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Draw one complete prescribed group on a tape.
Step 2: Represent the smaller available amount on the same scale.
Step 3: Partition both into common equal units.
Step 4: Compare the smaller amount with the whole group's size.
Step 5: Write the fractional quotient and verify by multiplication.
translations.commonMistakes: Calling a partial group zero ignores a valid fractional quantity. The result must reflect whether a fractional group makes sense in the context. 6 cups out of 9 is two-thirds of a batch, not zero batches merely because a full batch cannot be completed. Reversing reference rope C and rope D changes the ratio from 3 to 1/3.
translations.quickSummary: Quotients less than one represent fractional parts of a given group size.

lessons.sourceTitle: Open Up Resources 6–8 Math / IM 6–8 Math

translations.title: How Much in Each Group? (Part 1)
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will find the size of one group when a fractional number of groups is given.
Division may ask how much fits in one complete group when the total comes from a fractional number of identical groups. Draw a tape that represents the stated number of groups and scale up or down to one full group. This is different from counting how many fixed-size groups fit in a total.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- A ÷ n asks for one-group size when n equal groups share total A.
- A fractional number of groups can be scaled to one complete group.
- Check by multiplying the per-group size by the given number of groups.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: Three-quarters of a full container holds 6 liters. One full container holds 6 ÷ (3/4) = 8 liters.
Example 2: Two-thirds of a batch uses 4 cups flour. A whole batch uses 4 ÷ (2/3) = 6 cups.
Source batch-size task: Four cupcake batches need 6 cups flour, or 1½ cups for each whole batch. If one HALF batch of rolls needs 5/4 cups flour, the whole batch uses (5/4)÷(1/2)=5/2=2½ cups. Check (1/2)×(5/2)=5/4. Student-authored story and diagram need teacher review.
Example 3: First-party source bakery batches — Five full cookie batches use 10 cups flour, so 2 cups per batch; 4 cupcake batches using 6 cups require 1.5 cups each; one-half roll batch using 5/4 cups implies 5/2 cups for a full batch; and 2 cups making two-thirds of a bread batch implies 3 cups for a full batch. The denominator in each division is the NUMBER of batches rather than cups per batch.
Example 4: Water vessels with three different group counts — Fifteen cups evenly fill 2 bottles: 7.5 cups per bottle. Fifteen cups fill 1.5 identical pitchers: 10 cups per pitcher. Fifteen cups fill one-third of a pail: 45 cups per complete pail. Match each total to an original text-labeled tape; do not interchange the three denominators.
Example 5: Highway sections and parts — Three-quarter mile across two identical highway sections makes 3/8 mile per section. Three-quarter mile across 1.5 sections means 1/2 mile per section. If 3/4 mile is one-third of a particular section, the whole section is 9/4 or 2.25 miles. A teacher must review how the learner connects the stated PARTIAL number of sections with the complete unit.
Example 6: Infinite process modeling, not infinite decimal guessing — In a first-party middle-third coloring construction, after one coloring step one-third of a unit strip is colored; after the second step 1/3+2/9=5/9 is colored. After n such coloring steps, the total colored length is 1−(2/3)^n of the initial unit, so the colored share approaches 1 as n grows without reaching 1 at any finite step. The historical source labels the uncolored starting tape 'step 1', so the colored share at source step 10 is 1−(2/3)^9, NOT 1−(2/3)^10.
Description: Tape diagram. A first-party one-pitcher bar is partitioned into two equal halves. A total of 15 cups spans one whole pitcher plus one half-pitcher, labeled 1.5 pitchers; each half is 5 cups, and a full pitcher is 10 cups. Other diagrams showing 2 bottles and one-third pail require their own correctly labeled wholes.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Identify the fractional number of equal groups in the situation.
Step 2: Represent the given total as that fraction of a full tape.
Step 3: Partition or rescale from the fractional group to one full group.
Step 4: Compute total ÷ number of groups.
Step 5: Check by multiplying the full-group size by the original fractional count.
translations.commonMistakes: Dividing a total by the group size answers how many groups, whereas dividing by group count answers size per group; label the intended quantity. If 15 cups fill one-third of a pail, multiplying 15 by one-third is wrong; three thirds make a full pail, so the complete capacity is 45 cups. In a self-similar coloring construction finite steps never color the entire unit.
translations.quickSummary: Division can recover a complete group's size from a fractional number of groups.

lessons.sourceTitle: Open Up Resources 6–8 Math / IM 6–8 Math

translations.title: How Much in Each Group? (Part 2)
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will formulate and solve fraction-division questions from equal-group contexts.
A context can support different valid division questions. For a quantity of 3/4 liter, ask how many 1/8-liter portions it fills or how much each person receives if 3 people share it equally. The same total leads to different divisors and units; write the question before selecting an equation.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- The context must specify whether the divisor is a group size or group count.
- Fraction division must retain a consistent whole and equal parts.
- Teacher review can assess whether learner-created word questions match their equations.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: How many 1/8-liter portions fit into 3/4 liter? (3/4) ÷ (1/8) = 6 portions.
Example 2: If 3 people divide 3/4 liter equally, each gets (3/4) ÷ 3 = 1/4 liter. Check 3 × 1/4 = 3/4.
Example 3: First-party source dispenser reference — Three-quarters liter of water filling two-fifths of a dispenser implies full capacity (3/4)÷(2/5) = 15/8 or 1.875 liters. The 3/4 value measures WATER, while the 2/5 value measures the FRACTION of dispenser capacity. A tape showing five equal fifth-capacity sections has water in two sections; each fifth-section represents 3/8 liter.
Example 4: Unit-price and container tasks — Three and a half yards of fabric at $21 cost $6 per yard. If 4/9 kg baking soda costs $2, a full kilogram costs $2÷(4/9)=$4.50. Three liters in 1 1/5 equal bottles means 3÷(6/5)=2.5 liters per bottle. If 5/4 gallon fills 5/6 of a bucket, the full bucket is (5/4)÷(5/6)=3/2 or 1.5 gallons. Each answer names amount PER ONE of its actual unit.
Example 5: Compare quotient magnitude before computing — One-half divided by one-quarter is greater than 1; 1 divided by 3/4 is greater than 1; 2/3 divided by 7/8 is less than 1; and 2 7/8 divided by 2 3/5 is greater than 1. For a story matching (1/3)÷(1/4)=4/3, one-third cup of liquid contains one and one-third quarter-cup portions. Students may invent alternative equivalent contexts; their matching questions require teacher review.
Description: Tape diagram. One dispenser bar is divided into five equal segments, each representing three-eighths liter. Two segments are filled and together labeled three-fourths liter; all five segments sum to fifteen-eighths liters. The actual source picture and accessible container-fill visualization remain unverified.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Identify the quantity described in the context.
Step 2: Write a precise division question and name the missing quantity.
Step 3: Choose an equal-parts tape diagram.
Step 4: Write a division and matching multiplication equation.
Step 5: Find the answer with units, then review whether it answers the created question.
translations.commonMistakes: Writing an equation before clarifying the question may solve the wrong unknown. A learner-created story needs teacher rubric review, not only an arithmetic score. Two-fifths FULL means the water is not two-fifths of a liter; its absolute amount is 3/4 liter. A ratio of denominators depends on whether the divisor represents a fraction of a container or an item count.
translations.quickSummary: Fraction division supports both group-count and group-size questions; the mathematical interpretation determines the divisor.

lessons.sourceTitle: Open Up Resources 6–8 Math / IM 6–8 Math

translations.title: Dividing by Unit and Non-Unit Fractions
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will justify fraction division through unit-fraction diagrams and reciprocal multiplication.
To divide by a nonzero fraction a/b, first measure how many 1/b parts fit in the dividend, then group those small parts into bundles of a. This means multiplying the dividend by b and dividing by a, equivalently multiplying by the reciprocal b/a. The algorithm follows from a diagram, not from an unexplained rule.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- For positive a and b, x ÷ (a/b) = x × (b/a).
- The reciprocal transformation requires a nonzero divisor.
- Common-part diagrams explain why the numerator and denominator switch roles.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: To divide 3/4 by 2/3, count twelfths: the total is 9/12 and group size is 8/12. It is 9/8 = 1 1/8 groups. Reciprocal method: 3/4 × 3/2 = 9/8.
Example 2: For 2 ÷ 3/5, the two wholes contain ten fifths; group size is three fifths, giving 10/3 = 3 1/3 groups.
Source reciprocal connection: To ask how many 3s, 4s and 6s are in 12 gives 4, 3, 2; multiplying 12 by 1/3, 1/4 and 1/6 gives the same results. Discuss why dividing by a positive whole number is multiplying by its reciprocal. Extend to (3/4)÷(2/3)=9/8 and verify (9/8)×(2/3)=3/4.
Example 3: First-party unit-fraction partition tables — For fixed dividend 6, dividing by 1/2, 1/3, 1/4 and 1/6 gives 12, 18, 24, and 36. Extending to 1/8, 1/10 and 1/25 gives 48, 60 and 150. Generally a÷(1/b)=ab for nonzero b, justified by b equal tiny parts per whole and not merely remembered as an unexplained operation.
Example 4: Group fractional pieces for non-unit divisors — Six contains 18 one-third parts, and a 2/3-sized group consists of TWO of those parts, so 6÷(2/3)=18/2=9 groups. Likewise six contains 24 one-fourth parts: 6÷(3/4)=24/3=8 groups. Six contains 18 one-third parts: 6÷(4/3)=18/4=4.5 groups. Six÷(4/6) is also 9, since 4/6 equals 2/3.
Example 5: Reciprocal reasoning with partner roles — Partner A divides 12 by 3, 4 and 6 to obtain 4, 3 and 2; Partner B computes 12×(1/3), 12×(1/4) and 12×(1/6), obtaining the same values. For a general nonzero divisor b, x÷b=x×(1/b). If b is a nonzero fraction such as 3/4, the reciprocal must be 4/3, so six divided by three-quarters is 6×4/3=8. Teacher assessment checks both the diagram and why the inversion applies to the divisor.
Description: Ratio table. One column is labeled "fractional group size" with values 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/6, 2/3, 3/4, 4/3. A second column is labeled "number of groups in 6" with values 12, 18, 24, 36, 9, 8, 4.5. Explain how the numerator counts fractional unit pieces per group and why an improper fractional group can yield fewer groups.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Identify the dividend and nonzero fractional divisor.
Step 2: Represent both in common small units or a tape.
Step 3: Count fractional units in the total and in one group.
Step 4: Divide group counts or multiply by the reciprocal.
Step 5: Check by multiplying the quotient by the original divisor.
translations.commonMistakes: Invert-and-multiply without identifying which fraction is the divisor reverses the wrong number. Dividing by zero has no reciprocal and is undefined. Dividing 6 by two-thirds gives nine groups, not 18 (which counts one-third pieces only). Fractional group counts are valid; do not round 6÷(4/3)=4.5 to 4 without a contextual complete-group requirement.
translations.quickSummary: The reciprocal algorithm is justified by counting small fractional units and regrouping them into the specified divisor.

lessons.sourceTitle: Open Up Resources 6–8 Math / IM 6–8 Math

translations.title: Using an Algorithm to Divide Fractions
translations.explanation:
